QUESTIONS PRESENTED 


1. Whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of 
Columbia Circuit erred by holding, in direct conflict with five 
state courts of last resort, that an automobile manufacturer’s 
compliance with a Federal motor vehicle safety standard that 
permits, but does not require, installation of airbags in 
passenger vehicles preempts state common law ciaims that an 
automobile was defectively designed because it lacked an 
airbag? 


2. Whether the D.C. Circuit erred by holding that, 
because this Court engaged in implied preemption analysis in 
Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 U.S. 280 (1995), the lower 
courts are free to disregard the limitations on implied 
preemption most recently emphasized in Cipollone v. Liggett 
Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504 (1992), to find that a Federal motor 
vehicle safety standard promulgated pursuant to the National 
Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, 15 U.S.C. §§ 
1381-1431, impliedly preempts common law claims, even 
though the Act expressly provides that “[c]ompliance with any 
Federal motor vehicle safety standard . . . does not exempt any 
person from any liability under common law’’?

The parties to the proceedings below were petitioners 
Alexis Geier, William Geier, and Claire Geier (as appellants) 
and respondents American Honda Motor Company, Inc., Honda 


of America Manufacturing, Inc., and Honda Motor Company, 
Lid. (as appellees).

STATUTORY PROVISIONS INVOLVED 


The National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 
1966, as codified when the vehicle at issue in this case was 
manufactured, provided in pertinent part: 


15 U.S.C. § 1392(d). Supremacy of Federal 
standards; allowable higher standards for 
vehicles used by Federal or state 
_governments. Whenever a Federal motor 
vehicle safety standard established under this 
subchapter is in effect, no State or political 
subdivision of a State shall have any authority 
either to establish, or to continue in effect, with 
respect to any motor vehicle or item of motor 
vehicle equipment any safety standard 
applicable to the same aspect of performance of 
such vehicle or item of equipment which is not 
identical to the Federal standard. Nothing in 
this section shall be construed as preventing any 
State from enforcing any safety standard which 
is identical to a Federal safety standard. 
Nothing in this section shall be construed to 
prevent the Federal Government or the 
government of any State or political subdivision 


thereof from establishing a safety requirement 
applicable to motor vehicles or motor vehicle 
equipment procured for its own use if such 
requirement imposes a higher standard of 
performance than that required to comply with 
the otherwise applicable Federal standard. 


15 U.S.C. § 1397(k). Continuation of 
common law liability. Compliance with any 
Federal motor vehicle safety standard issued 
under this subchapter does not exempt any 
person from any liability under common law. 


On July 5, 1994, Congress recodified the Act “without 
substantive change” (Pub. L. No. 103-272, 108 Stat. 745, 941). 
The new Code provisions, in relevant part, are as follows: 


49 U.S.C. § 30103. Relationship to other 
laws. 


(b) Preemption. (1) When a motor vehicle 
safety standard is in effect under this chapter, a 
State or a political subdivision of a State may 
prescribe or continue in effect a standard 
applicable to the same aspect of performance of 
a motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment 
only if the standard is identical to the standard 
prescribed under this chapter. However, the 
United States Government, a State, or a political 
subdivision of a State may prescnie a standard 
for a motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment 
obtained for its own use that imposes a higher 
performance requirement than that required by 


2 


the otherwise 4pplicable standard under this 
chapter. 


(2) A State may enforce a standard that is 
identical to a standard prescribed under this 
chapter. 


(e) Common Law Liability. Compliance 
with a motor vehicle safety standard prescribed 
under this chapter does not exempt a person 
from liability at common law. 


All of the applicable preemption cases, including the 
decisions by the two courts below, discuss the provisions as 
codified before the 1994 recodification. This petition, therefore, 
uses the citations employed in those decisions. 


STATEMENT OF THE CASE 


On January 16, 1992, Alexis Geier was operating a 1987 
Honda Accord in the District of Columbia. Ms. Geier was 
wearing the manual three-point lap belt and shoulder harness 
provided for the driver in the design of the car. Rounding a 
curve, the vehicle spun out of control and collided with a tree. 
Despite the fact that she was wearing the available lap belt and 
shoulder harness, Ms. Geier sustained grievous and serious 
head injuries. See App. 2; Complaint ff 4-7, 18-21. 


When the 1987 Honda Accord at issue in this case was 
manufactured a federal regulation promulgated pursuant to the 
National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, 15 


U.S.C. §§ 1381 et seg. (“the Safety Act’’) —i.e., Federal Motor 
Vehicle Safety Standard 208 — gave Honda the option to install 


3 


airbags in its car. See 49 C.F.R. § 571.208. Specifically, for 
cars manufactured between September 1, 1986, and September 
1, 1987, Standard 208 required Honda, at a minimum, to install 
some form of passive restraint in a specified percentage of its 
cars and to install at least a manual three-point lap belt and 
shoulder harness in the remaining percentage. Jd. See also 
App. 3. It also allowed all manufacturers to do more than the 
bare minimum required (including installing both an airbag and 
a manual three-point lap belt and shoulder harness in all cars). 


On January 12, 1995, Ms. Geier and her parents filed 
this lawsuit seeking damages under the common law of the 
District of Columbia against respondents American Honda 
Motor Company, Inc., Honda of America Manufacturing, Inc., 
and Honda Motor Company, Ltd. (collectively, “Honda”) on 
theories of negligence, breach of warranty, and strict product 
liability. The Geiers alleged that the 1987 Honda Accord was 
negligently and defectively designed and that, if the car had 
contained a driver’s-side airbag in addition to the manual lap 
belt and shoulder harness, Ms. Geier would not have been 
seriously injured in the crash. 


Even though the design advocated by petitioners was 
fully consistent with Standard 208, Honda moved for summary 
judgment on the ground that the Geiers’ claims were preempted 
by the Safety Act and Standard 208. App. 17. In response, 
petitioners pointed out, inter alia, that the Safety Act explicitly 


' As the lower court observed, the requirements of Standard 208 
have since become more stringent. After September 1, 1989, car 
manufacturers had to install either an airbag or an automatic seatbelt that 
would signal the driver with a warning light if the belt became unhooked. 
App. 3. Currently, passenger cars manufactured after September 1, 1997, 
must have “an inflatable restraint system at the driver’s and right front 
passenger’s position.” App. 3. 


provides that “[c]ompliance with any Federal motor vehicle 
standard . . . does not exempt any person from any liability 
under common law.” 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k). On December 10, 
1997, however, the district court found that petitioners’ claims 
were preempted on the theory that a jury verdict in their favor 
might establish a safety standard that was not identical to 
Standard 208. App. 17-20. 


The court of appeals affirmed. App. 1-16. In its 
decision, the court first acknowledged that any conclusion that 
petitioners’ claims are expressly preempted would be 
“problematic” in light of both the Act’s “broadly worded 
savings clause” and the strong presumption against finding 
express preemption of common law claims when Congress’ 
intent to preempt “is not clear from the statute’s language.” 
App. 10-11. Given the broad wording of the savings clause, 
the court reasoned, “it would be difficult to discern a ‘clear and 
manifest purpose of Congress’ to preempt a design defect claim 
based on the absence of an airbag.” App. 1 1 (citations omitted). 


The court of appeals ultimately decided that it need not 
resolve the express preemption question, however, since it 
found instead that petitioners’ claims are impliedly preempted 
by Standard 208. App. 12. The court first rejected petitioners’ 
claim that, under Cipollone v. Liggett Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504 
(1992), the Safety Act’s express provisions addressing the 
scope of preemption bar any inquiry into implied preemption. 
After acknowledging that Cipollone does contain language to 
that effect (App. 12), the court held that this Court’s subsequent 
decision in Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 U.S. 280 (1995), 
repudiated Cipollone’s apparent holding that implied 
preemption may not be considered in cases where — as here — 
the statute itself expressly defines the scope of preemption. 
App. 12-13. 


The court went on to hold that petitioners’ claims are 
impliedly preempted on the ground that they conflict with 
federal law. While conceding that Standard 208 “does not 
mandate or forbid the use of airbags” (App. 14), the court 
adopted Honda’s argument that imposition of common law 
liability for failure to install an airbag would interfere with the 
federal government’s decision to make airbags only “one of 
several options car manufacturers could choose to comply with 
the passive restraint requirement of Standard 208 . . ..” App. 
15. Creation of these options, the court reasoned, was integra! 
to the federal government’s policy “of encouraging both public 
acceptance of the airbag technology and experimentation with 
better passive restraint systems.” App. 15. Because common 
law liability for failing to install an airbag could “interfere with 
the regulatory method” embodied in Standard 208, the court 
concluded that petitioners’ claims are “implicitly pre-empted” 
by the Act. App. 16. 


REASONS FOR GRANTING THE WRIT 


When Congress enacted the Safety Act in 1966, it 
unequivocally stated the preemptive effect that compliance with 
a Federal safety standard was to have on common law liability: 
“Compliance with any Federal motor vehicle safety standard 
issued under this subchapter does not exempt any person from 
any liability under common law.” 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k) 
(emphasis added). The D.C. Circuit’s preemrtion decision 
contravenes these plain words and conflicts with the ruling of 
five state courts of last resort to address this preemption issue. 
The lower court’s ruling also demonstrates, and increases, the 
confusion created by this Court’s decision in Myrick about the 
Safety Act’s preemptive effect. Finally, the decision below 
incorrectly answers an important federal question that has not 
been. but should be, decided by this Court: whether Congress 
intended the Safety Act to preempt state common law claims. 


6 


This Court shou'd grant review to resolve the conflict among 
the federal courts of appeal and state courts of last resort, 
eliminate the confusion caused by Myrick, and decide whether 
Congress’ words mean what they say. 


1. The Decision Below Conflicts With the 
Decisions of Five State Courts of Last Resort. 


The Court of Appeals’ decision expands and exacerbates 
the growing conflict among the federal courts of appeals and 
the state courts of last resort over the Safety Act’s preemptive 
effect with respect to clain > that an automobile is defective 
because it lacks an airbag. Only this Court can bring the 
conflict to an end. If this Court does not step in, the conflict 
will only get worse, as the decision below reflects. 


To date, five federal courts of appeals and two state 
courts of last resort have held that common law claims based on 
the absence of an airbag are preempted by federal law. See 
Harris v. Ford Motor Co., 110 F.3d 1410 (9th Cir. 1997); 
Montag v. Honda Motor Co., 75 F.3d 1414 (10th Cir.), cert. 
denied, 519 U.S. 814 (1996); Pokorny v. Ford Motor Co., 902 
F.2d 1116 (3d Cir.), cert. denied, 498 U.S. 853 (1990); Taylor 
v. General Motors Corp., 875 F.2d 816 (11th Cir. 1989), cert. 
denied, 494 U.S. 1065 (1990);? Wood v. General Motors Corp., 
865 F.2d 395 (ist Cir. 1988), cert. denied, 494 U.S. 1065 
(1990); Cellucci v. General Motors Corp., 706 A.2d 806 (Pa. 


As the lower court noted, “{tJhe Eleventh Circuit recently 
reaffirmed Taylor. In /rving, the court noted that although its decision in 
Myrick v. Fruehauf Corp. stated that Taylor had been abrogated in part, see 
136 F.3d at 767 n.1 (citing Myrick, 13 F.3d 1516, 1521-22 (11th Cir. 1994)), 
subsequent Supreme Court precedent made clear that ‘Taylor 1s correct and 
can be used for evaluating pre-emption of state law.’ /d." App. 7. 


5 


—- Cooper v. General Motors Corp., 702 So.2d 428 (Miss. 


In each of these cases, as here, “Standard 208 did not 
require airbags for the model-year cars in question, but 
presented them as one of several options from which 
manufacturers could choose.” App. 7. And, with the exception 
of the Ninth Circuit in Harris (v"...\ found express preemption 
of no-airbag claims), in each case, as here, the court concluded 
that the plaintiffs’ claims were impliedly preempted because 
they conflicted with federal law.’ 


These decisions are flatly contrary to the holdings of 
five state courts of last resort that the Safety Act does not 
preempt no-airbag claims. First, in 1995, the New Hampshire 
Supreme Court unanimously held in Ford Motor Co. v. 
Tebbetts, 665 A.2d 345 (N.H. 1995), cert. denied, 516 U.S. 
1072 (1996), that the Safety Act expressly preserves all 
common law claims; that Congress’ plain words preclude any 
finding of implied preemption; and that auto manufacturers can 
thererore be sued under common law for defective designs that 
lacked airbags. 


Later the same year, in Wilson v. Pleasant and General 
Motors Corp., 660 N.E.2d 327 (Ind. 1995), the Supreme Court 
of Indiana agreed in all respects — and held that, even if implied 
preemption could be reached, there is no conflict between a no- 
airbag claim and Standard 208 because, inter alia, “[Standard] 


i In Cooper, the Mississippi Supreme Court stated in dicta that 
there might be express preemption as well, but it ultimately decided the case 
on imphed preemption grounds. See 702 So.2d at 434. (“In the case sub 
judice, there appears to be both express preemption, under § 1392(d), and 
umplied preemption . . . [but] this Court will filter this case through an 
implied preemption gnd.”). 


208 does not prohibit airbags — it only permits some other 
alternatives.” Jd. at 337. 


Since that time, the Supreme Court of Arizona, the 
Supreme Court of Ohio, and the New York Court of Appeals 
have all followed suit, holding that an automobile manufacturer 
may be sued for failure to install airbags in its vehicles. See 
Munroe v. Galati, 938 P.2d 1114 (Ariz. 1997) (finding no 
express or implied preemption of no-airbag claim); Minton v. 
Honda of America Mfg., Inc., 684 N.E.2d 648 (Ohio 1997) 
(same); Drastel v. Toyota Motor Corp., 699 N.E.2d 376 (N.Y. 
1998) (same). 


Thus, there is a deep split among a host of federal and 
state courts of last resort regarding the precise question 
presented in this case: whether a manufacturer may be sued for 
failing to install airbags in one of its vehicles.* Notably, 
virtually all of these courts agree that there could be no express 
preemption of common law claims under the Safety Act.’ This 


* The lower federal cou ts and state trial and appellate courts are 
also deeply split on this issue. See generally Cellucci, 706 A.2d at 812 n.4 
(collecting cases); Cooper v. General Motors Corp., 702 So.2d at 433-34 
(same). 


* As noted above, the only exception among the federal courts of 
appeals is the Ninth Circuit's decision in Harris, 110 F.3d at 1416, holding 
express preemption of no-airbag claims. There 1s also dicta to that effect in 
the Mississippi Supreme Court's decision in Cooper, 702 So.2d at 434. See 
n.3, supra. We note, however, that a number of state and federal lower 
courts have held that there is express preemption of no-airbag claims. See 
generally Cellucci, 706 A.2d at 812 n.4 (collecting cases). In a different 
context, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit has recently held 
that common law claims involving a defective windshield are expressly 
preempted by the Safety Act. See Garcia v. Volvo Europe Truck, N.V., 112 
F.3d 291, 297 (7th Cir. 1997), cert. denied, 113 S. Ct. 697 (1998). The 
Supreme Court of Idaho has also concluded that the Safety Act expressly

is not surprising, given that the Act’s savings clause explicitly 
provides that “[cjompliance with any Federal motor vehicle 
standard . . . does not exempt any person from any liability 
under common law.” 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k). As the New York 
Court of Appeals stated in Drattel, this language “potently and 


pointedly negates any lingering notion of express preemption 
of state common-law claims.” 699 N.E.2d at 382. 


These courts differ, however, over the extent to which 
no-airbag claims are impliedly preempted by virtue of a conflict 
with federal law. Five state courts of last resort have held that, 
in view of the Safety Act’s remarkably clear savings clause, it 
is unnecessary to even reach the question of implied 
preemption. See Tebbetts, 665 A.2d at 348; Munroe, 938 P.2d 
at 1117-18; Minton, 684 N.E.2d at 658; Drattel, 699 N.E.2d at 
382-83; Wilson, 660 N.E.2d at 334-36. In these courts’ view, 
Congress’ plain words on the subject are both the beginning and 
end of the matter: the Safety Act does not under any 
circumstance preempt common law claims.° 


On the other hand, four federal appellate courts and two 
state supreme courts have either rejected or failed even to 
consider the possibility that the Act’s express language

preempts a claim that a car is defectively designed because it lacks a lap

conflict with all of the other cases cited herein — including the decision 
below — that reject the argument that the Safety Act expressly preempts

Taylor, 875 F.2d at 825-26; Wood, 865 F.2d at 414-16;

This ongoing dispute about the Safety Act’s preemptive 
effect has serious practical consequences. There are currently 
thousands of automobile design defect lawsuits pending 
throughout the nation, hundreds of which involve the 
manufacturers’ failure to install lap belts, shoulder harnesses, 
and/or airbags. The preemption issue has been raised or is 
lurking in all of these cases. The legal and judicial resources 
being spent on this issue are mushrooming, with no end to the 
conflict in sight. 


It is clear, moreover, that the time is ripe for this Court 
to resolve the conflict for once and for all. Eleven years ago, in 
response to a petition for certiorari in Wood v. General Motors 
Corp., 865 F.2d 395 (ist Cir. 1988) (finding no-airbag claims 
preempted by federal law), this Court invited the United States 
to express its views as to whether review was warranted. In 
given the lack of a conflict among the federal courts of appeals 
or state courts of last resort. See Wood v. General Motors 
Corp., No. 89-46 (October Term, 1989), Brief for the United 
States as Amicus Curiae, at 16-17. The petition was ultimately 
denied. See 494 U.S. 1065 (1990). 


In the wake of Wood, this Court declined to revisit the 
issue of preemption under the Safety Act until it granted review 
of the Eleventh Circuit’s decision in Myrick v. Freuhauf, 13 
F.3d 1516 (11th Cir. 1994). At first glance, Myrick appeared to 
present an opportunity for this Court to decide the same 
question presented here: i.e., whether no-airbag claims are 


11 


preempted by federal law.’ As it turned out, however, Myrick 
involved an entirely different aspect of vehicle performance — 
anti-lock brakes in trucks — as to which there was no federal 
regulatory standard in place. See 514 U.S. 280, 286 (1995); 
App. 6. This Court ultimately issued an extremely narrow 
ruling finding no express or implied preemption because of the 
absence of any applicable federal regulation. See id. at 286-90. 
Thus, Myrick did not decide what the preemptive effect of the 
Safety Act would be in cases where — as here — the federal 
government has regulated in the area. 


In the years since Myrick, the issue of airbag preemption 
the New Hampshire Supreme Court held that no-airbag claims 
are not preempted by federal law. See Tebbetts, 665 A.2d 345. 
The following year, the Tenth Circuit held precisely the 
opposite. See Montag, 75 F.3d 1414. Although both Tebbetts 
and Montag raised the no-airbag preemption issue, review was 
arguably premature since they were the first rulings issued by 
a state court of last resort and a U.S. Court of Appeals since this 
decisions in Tebbetts and Montag were permitted to stand. 


Since that time, however, a post-Myrick split has 
developed and grown increasingly deep, with two more federal

issue that was presented, but ultimately left unanswered, by

2. The Conflict Below Stems Primarily from 
Confusion About the Proper Approach to 


Preemption Analysis that Only this Court 
Can Resolve. 


The lower courts’ ongoing disagreement about the 
Safety Act’s preemptive effect largely stems from confusion 
created by this Court’s decision in Myrick over an important 
question of federal law: whether common law claims may ever 
be impliedly preempted under the Safety Act or any other 
explicitly preserving the precise aspect of state law at issue. To 
appreciate why Myrick caused such confusion, it is essential to 
understand the context in which that decision took place. 


. For 20 years after the Safety Act’s 1966 enactment, the 
nation’s appellate courts unanimously agreed that the Safety 
Act does not preempt common law claims.’ In 1986, however,

Before this Court had an opportunity to overturn these

argued in the past, that it was exempt from common law 
liability because it had complied with a Federal motor vehicle 
safety standard — specifically, Standard 208 governing occupeut 
restraints. In a two-to-one decision, the First Circuit explicitly 
adopted the rationale of Palmer, its then-recent cigarette 
labeling decision, and became the first appeals court in the 
nation to find a common law claim impliedly (but not 
expressly) preempted by the Safety Act, despite Congress’ clear 
statement of anti-preemptive intent. Wood, 865 F.2d at 410-11. 
In the next three years, the Third, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits 
(and several lower courts) followed, albeit on varying 
rationales. See Pokorny, 902 F.2d at 1116; Kitts v. General 
Motors Corp., 875 F.2d 787 (10th Cir. 1989), cert. denied, 494 
U.S. 1065 (1990); Taylor, 875 F.2d at 816. 


In 1992, however, this Court issued its decision in 
Cipollone v. Liggett Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504, explicitly

Cipollone effectively overruled the various federal court

In Myrick, this Court reviewed the first decision by a

Safety Act’s preemptive effect in the wake of Cipollone. See 
Myrick v. Freuhauf Corp., 13 F.3d 1516 (11th Cir. 1994). As 
noted above, however, Myrick did not involve a no-airbag 
claim; rather, the case was a common law tort action for failure 
to install anti-lock brakes in a truck. /d. at 1518. And, unlike 
the no-airbag cases, which revolve around an alleged conflict 
between common law claims and Standard 208, there was no 
federal regulatory standard in effect governing anti-lock brakes 
in trucks. See App. 6. The Eleventh Circuit’s decision, 
however, did not address this factual difference; instead, the 
court analyzed the case as though it involved a no-airbag claim. 
See 13 F.3d at 1519-22. It then reversed its prior holding in 
Taylor, 875 F.2d 816, that no-airbag claims are impliedly 
preempted under the Safety Act and Standard 208. In so doing, 
the Eleventh Circuit held that it was obligated to overturn 
Taylor in light of “Cipollone’s clear instruction that when there 
is aN express pre-emption provision we should not consider 
implied pre-emption . . ..”. 13 F.3d at 1522. 


This Court granted review to decide whether the Safety 
Act preempts common law claims that allegedly conflict with 
federal standards. See supra at n.7. However, this Court 
ultimately did not decide the issue because, as became apparent 
after review was granted, there was simply no federal safety 
standard in effect governing anti-lock brakes in trucks. Noting 
that the Safety Act’s preemption clause “applies only 
‘[w]henever a Federal motor vehicle safety standard is in 
effect,” Myrick held that the absence of any federal standard 
foreclosed any finding of express preemption. 514 U.S. at 286- 
87. This Court accordingly declined to even consider whether 
the Act’s savings clause expressly preserved all common law 
claims, id. at 287 n.3, or whether the Safety Act and Standard 


16 


208 would impliedly preempt a claim that an automobile is 
defective because it lacks an airbag. /d. at 289-90. 


Myrick, however, went on to create massive confusion 
by rejecting as “without merit” the Eleventh’s Circuit’s holding 
Congress has chosen to include an express preemption clause 
in a statute.” Jd. at 287. In an attempt to clarify the proper 
approach to preemption analysis, Myrick stated as follows: 


The fact that an express definition of the pre- 
emptive reach of a statute “implies” — i.e., 
supports a reasonable inference — that Congress 
did not intend to pre-empt other matters does 
not mean that the express clause entirely 
ferscloses any possibility of implied preemption 
... At best, Cipollone supports an inference 
that an express preemption clause forecloses 
implied preemption; it does not establish a rule. 


Id. at 288-89. 


In regard to Cipollone, these statements made perfect 
sense. The two statutes at issue in Cipollone contained express 
preemption clauses (but, unlike, the Safety Act, no express 
savings clause). The fact that Congress thought to include 
those express clauses in the cigarette labeling statutes did not, 
without more, necessarily mean that Congress also thought of 
all other aspects of state law that might be preempted by the 
statutes — and intended to preserve them. 


In the Safety Act, however, there is more than just an 
express preemption clause. There is an express anti-preemption 
clause explicitly preserving all common law claims. In Myrick, 
however, this Court did not address that fact, since it had 


17 


already deemed it unnecessary to decide the meaning of the 
savings clause given the absence of any federal regulatory 
standard governing anti-lock brakes. Instead, it simply said that 
the Eleventh Circuit’s interpretation of Cipollone was “without 
merit” and then made the statements quoted above. As a result, 
Myrick has caused extensive confusion as to whether the Safety 
Act’s express language precludes a finding of implied 
preemption in cases where — as here — there is a federal 
regulatory standard in place. 


Thus, for example, five state courts of last resort have 
found that Myrick still “permits an inference” that, where 
Congress has clearly and unequivocally expressed an intention 
not to preempt common law claims, there can be no finding of 
implied preemption. Munroe, 938 P.2d at 1118. See also 
Tebbetts, 665 A.2d at 348; Minton, 684 N.E.2d at 658; Draitel, 
699 N.E.2d at 382-83; Wilson, 660 N.E.2d at 334-36. In these 
courts’ view, “Myrick did not overrule Cipollone. Rather, it is 
apparent that Myrick sought merely to disapprove of decisions 
interpreting Cipollone to mean that implied preemption can 
never exist when Congress has included an express preemption 
clause in the legislation in question.” Minton, 684 N.E.2d at 
658. See also Wilson, 660 N.E.2d at 336 (Myrick simply 
clarified that the mere existence of “an express preemption 
clause does not as a rule foreclose implied preemption.”) These 
courts went on to hold, however, that the Safety Act’s savings 
clause is so clear and unambiguous with respect to Congress’ 
intent to preserve common law claims that any finding of 
implied preemption is foreclosed.'°

courts went on to consider (and reject) the implied preemption claims.

In short, in the time since Myrick “clarified” the

infected preemption analysis in Safety Act cases involving

Equally important, assuming that implied preemption 
can properly be considered, this case enables the Court to make 
clear that no-airbag claims are not impliedly preempted. 
Simply put, there is no conflict between petitioners’ claims and 
Standard 208. It is true that Standard 208 required all 1987 
model-year cars to have, at a minimum, either (1) a manual lap 
belt and shoulder harness, (2) an automatic belt system 
providing at least a specified level of protection in head-on 
crashes, or (3) an airbag or other device providing automatic 
protection in head-on and angular crashes. But is also true that 
Honda, which chose the first option, could have installed an 
airbag in the car driven by Ms. Geier in addition to the manual 
lap-belt and shoulder harness it installed, and still have 
complied with that option under Standard 208. And it is 
obvious that, if Honda had taken that step, Ms. Geier would 
have been safer. If, by failing to install an airbag, Honda 
violated the common law of the District of Columbia and 
caused Ms. Geier’s injuries, Congress did not intend to exempt 
Honda from liability. Section 1397(k) makes that fact plain. 


The lack of a conflict between petitioners’ claims and 
federal law is made even clearer by the regulatory history of 
Standard 208, which is devoid of any suggestion that the federal 
government intended to preempt airbag-related common law 
claims. To the contrary, when it promulgated the version of 
Standard 208 applicable in this case, the federal government 
said that the design that petitioners assert Honda should have 
used in its car offered the most safety benefits of any occupant 
restraint system. See 49 Fed. Reg. at 28,986 (1984) (“[T]he 
most effective system is an airbag plus a lap and shoulder 
belt.”). The regulatory preamble specifically noted that 
manufacturers would be prompted to use the best system by, 


26 


among other things, the threat of “potential liability for any 
defunct system.” Jd. at 29,000. And it tellingly quoted - 
without disagreement — the formal comment of a public health 
official that “[p]eople whose crash injury would have been 
averted had the car been equipped with an airbag can sue the car 
manufacturer to recover the dollar value of the injury.” Jd. at 
28,972. 


That is precisely what petitioners seek to do here. This 
Court has repeatedly refused to find that Congress intended to 
deprive tort victims of common law remedies, even when 
Congress has not expressly preserved common law claims, 
saying “it is difficult to believe that Congress would, without 
comment, remove all means of judicial recourse for those 
injured by illegal conduct.” Medtronic, 116 S. Ct. at 2251 
(citing Silkwood v. Kerr-McGee Corp., 464 U.S. 238, 251 
(1984)). In this case, Congress did comment and it expressly 
preserved all common law claims. The Court should grant 
review to ensure that Congress’ intent is respected and that the 
Geiers — and thousands of similarly situated Americans — are 
not illegally denied their day in court. 


27 


CONCLUSION 


This petition for writ of certiorari should be granted.

Before: WILLIAMS, GINSBURG and ROGERS, Circuit Judges. 
Opinion for the Court filed by Circuit Judge ROGERS. 


ROGERS, Circuit Judge: The question on appeal is 
whether federal law pre-empts a defective design lawsuit 
against the American Honda Motor Company for damages 
arising from injuries suffered by Alexis Geier' when her 1987 
Honda Accord, which did not have an airbag, crashed into a 
tree. The district court granted summary judgment for Honda 
on the ground that the lawsuit was pre-empted by the National 
Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, as amended, 
15 U.S.C. § 1381 et seg. (Safety Act), and the Federal Motor 
Vehicle Safety Standard 208, 49 C.F.R. § 571.208 (1997) 
(Standard 208), which govern the passive safety restraints that 
automobile manufacturers must install.’ Joining our sister 
circuits, we affirm, concluding that Geier’s lawsuit is 
impliedly pre-empted. 


Under the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, the 
laws of the United States “shall be the supreme Law of the 
Land; . . . any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State 
to the Contrary notwithstanding.” U.S. Const. art. VI, cl. 2. 
In applying this Clause, courts have identified three ways in 


' Appellants are Alexis Geier, a minor at the time of the accident, 
and her parents, William and Claire Geier. For ease of reference we refer 
to appellants as “Geier.” 


? The Safety Act is now codified at 49 U.S.C. § 30101 ef seq.

however, were made “without substantive change” to the underlying 
provisions. See Pub. L. No. 103-272, § Ma), 108 Stat. 745, 745 (1994). 
Because the relevant circuit courts of appeal decisions, the district court, and 
the parties all use the old designations, we will use them as well. 


App. 2 


which a federal statute or regulation can pre-empt state law: 
by express pre-emption, by “field” pre-emption (in which 
Congress regulates the field “so extensively that [it] clearly 
intends the subject area to be controlled only by federal law’’), 
and by implied or conflict pre-emption, which applies when a 
state law conflicts with a federal statute or. regulation. /rving 
v. Mazda Motor Corp., 136 F.3d 764, 767 (11th Cir. 1998); 
see also Cipollone v. Liggett Group, 505 U.S. 504, 516 
(1992). The Supreme Court has identified two presumptions 
that courts must consider when invoking the doctrine of pre- 
emption. First, in areas where States have exercised their 
historic police powers (such as the health and safety of their 
citizens), courts must start with a presumption against pre- 
emption, absent a “clear and manifest purpose of Congress.” 
Medtronic, Inc. v. Lohr, 518 U.S. 470, 485 (1996) (quoting 
Rice v. Santa Fe Elevator Corp., 331 U.S. 218, 230 (1947)). 
Second, in every pre-emption case, “[t]he purpose of Con- 
gress is the ultimate touchstone.” /d. (quoting Retail Clerks v. 
Schennerhorn, 375 U.S. 96, 103 (1963)). 


For cars manufactured between September 1, 1986, and 
September 1, 1987, the inclusion of a driver-side airbag was 
one of several passive restraint “options” from which car 
manufacturers could choose in order to comply with Standard 
208.’ See 49 C.F.R. § 571.208, $4.1.3.1.1 (1997). The effect 
of Standard 208 on state law is governed by two provisions of

571.208, $4.1.5.3 (1997). See generally Wood v. General Motors Corp.,

As noted, Geier contends that § 1392(k) expressly pre-

1392(d) expressly preempts state safety standards not 
‘identical’ to applicable federal standards.” In Honda’s view, 
because Standard 208 allowed car manufacturers the option of 
choosing an airbag, a jury verdict in favor of Geier on her

comply with a different standard.’ 


The language of § 1392(d) is fairly sweeping, providing 
that when a federal motor vehicle safety standard is in effect, 
“no State or political subdivision of a State shall have any 
authority either to establish, or to continue in effect, with 
respect to any motor vehicle or item of motor vehicle 
equipment any safety standard applicable to the same aspect 
of performance of such vehicle or item of equipment which is 
not identical to the Federal standard.” 15 U.S.C. § 1392(d) 
(emphasis added). At a minimum, this language restricts a 
State’s authority to enact legislation or regulations that 
affirmatively require car manufacturers to adopt standards not 
identical to Standard 208. See Wood, 865 F.2d at 408. In 
other words, a State could not require, by statute or 
regulation, that a car manufacturer install airbags in models 
for which Standard 208 makes them only an option. 


* However, Geier’s contention that the term “safety standard” in

Ultimately, we need not resolve whether Geier’s claim is 
expressly pre-empted, however, because we conclude that a 
verdict in her favor would stand as an obstacle to the federal 
government’s chosen method of achieving the Act’s safety 
objectives, and consequently, the Act impliedly pre-empts her 
lawsuit. The conclusion arises largely from the position 
advanced by Honda, in the alternative, that state jury verdicts 
that hold manufacturers liable for not installing airbags will 
create a conflict with Standard 208. 


As a threshold matter, we are unpersuaded by Geier’s 
contention, relying on Cipollone, that the court cannot reach 
the implied pre-emption argument because congressional in- 
tent is expressly stated in § 1397(k), which saves all common 
law claims from pre-emption, and therefore only express pre- 
emption analysis is applicable. It is true that the Supreme 
Court in Cipollone observed that when Congress has included 
a provision explicitly addressing the issue of pre-emption, and

congressional intent with respect to state authority, 
there is no need to infer congressional intent to pre-

Circuits have criticized the Wood court's express pre-emption analysis,

ted). But the Supreme Court has also rejected Geier’s 
interpretation. In Myrick, the Court noted that some circuit 
courts of appeal had read Cipollone to mean that “implied 
pre-emption cannot exist when Congress has chosen to in- 
clude an express pre-emption clause in a statute. This argu- 
ment is without merit.” Myrick, 514 U.S. at 287. The Court 
instructed that the presence of “an express definition of the 
pre-emptive reach of a statute” only creates a reasonable 
inference “that Congress did not intend to pre-empt other 
matters.” /d. at 288. Such a clause does not “entirely 
foreclose[ }] any possibility of implied pre-emption.” /d. 


The tension between §§ 1392(d) and 1397(k) prevents 
the identification of any “express definition” of the reach of 
pre-emption in the Safety Act. Furthermore, in Myrick the 
Supreme Court engaged in implied pre-emption analysis of 
the Safety Act after concluding that § 1392(d) did not “ex- 
pressly extinguish state tort law” for no-ABS claims. /d. at 
287; see also Montag, 75 F.3d at 1417. Rejecting the 
argument that Cipollone barred consideration of implied pre- 
emption in all cases involving express pre-emption language, 
the Supreme Court concluded that no implied pre-emption 
existed on the facts before it because “there is simply no 
federal standard for a private party to comply with.” Myrick, 
514 U.S. at 289. Therefore, Cipollone does not bar this court 
trom considering Honda’s implied pre-emption argument. 

Implied conflict pre-emption occurs “where it is 
impossible for a private party to comply with both state and 


federal requirements, . . . or where state law stands as an 
obstacle to the accomplishment and execution of the full 


App. 13 


purposes and objectives of Congress.” Jd. at 287 (internal 
quotation marks omitted). Federal regulations, as well as 
federal statutes, can pre-empt conflicting state law. Pokorny, 
902 F.2d at 1122; see also Fidelity Fed. Sav. & Loan Assn v. 
de la Cuesta, 458 U.S. 141, 153 (1982). Unlike Myrick, in 
which the Supreme Court found no implied pre-emption, see 
514 U.S. at 288, the instant case involves a federal safety 
standard thet governs the use of airbags in 1987 model-year 
cars. Although the standard does not mandate or forbid the 
use of airbags, it presents them as one of several options from 
which manufacturers may choose. While Geier maintains not 
unpersuasively that a design defect lawsuit based on the 
absence of an airbag does not conflict with Standard 208 
because Honda can be held accountable under state law for 
failing to do more than the minimum required by the option it 
chose (i.e. installing a manual seat belt with a warning light), 
her argument fails to surmount the obstacle that a favorable 
verdict would present to achieving congressional objectives in 
the chosen manner. As the First Circuit observed in Wood, 
allowing liability for the absence of airbags would “interfere[ 
] with the method by which Congress intended to meet” its 
goal of increasing automobile safety. Wood, 865 F.2d at 408. 
A successful nu-airbag claim would mean that an automobile 
without an airbag was defectively designed. Congress, how- 
ever, delegated authority to prescribe specific motor vehicle 
safety standards to the Secretary of Transportation, see 49 
U.S.C. § 30111(a) (1994), who in turn explicitly rejected 
requiring airbags in all cars on the ground that a more flexible 
approach would better serve public safety. 49 Fed. Reg. 
28,962, 29,000-02 (1984). 


The tortured history of Section 208 demonstrates that 
federal regulators have vaci'lated on the relative merits of 
requiring or including airbags in passenger vehicles. See 
Wood, 865 F.2d at 398-99. It also reveals how far public 


App. 14 


acceptance of air bags has come and, concomitantly, the 
success of the Secretary’s decision on how to implement the 
Act. When the Secretary promulgated the regulations at issue 
in this case, she rejected an all-airbag rule out of concern that 
notwithstanding the safety benefits of airbags, the public 
might respond negatively to the unfamiliar technology if it 
was required in all cars. 49 Fed. Reg. at 28,989. In the 
Secretary’s view, gradually phasing in airbags could po- 
tentially address “unfounded” fears among members of the 
a choice among passive restraint systems would expose them 
to the benefits of the airbag technology. /d. at 28,988, 
29,001. Cf State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Dole, 802 
F.2d 474, 488-89 (D.C. Cir. 1986). At the same time, the 


Secretary was concerned that not affording manufacturers 


discretion to install an automatic occupant restraint system 
ran the risk of impeding the development of more effective 
protective systems. 49 Fed. Reg. at 29,001. Thus, a 
performance standard making airbags one of several options 
car manufacturers could choose to comply with the passive 
restraint requirements of Standard 208, rather than mandating 
specific use of one safety device, would advance public safety 
in two respects, by allowing consumers to adjust to the new 
technology and by permitting experimentation with designs 
for even safer systems. 49 Fed. Reg. at 28,988, 28,997. 


With this history in mind, and consistent with the policy 
decision made by the Secretary, we conclude that allowing 
design defect claims based on the absence of an airbag for the 
model-year car at issue would frustrate the Department’s 
policy of encouraging both public acceptance of the airbag 
technology and experimentation with better passive restraint 
systems. Even if the Secretary’s gradual adoption of an 
airbag requirement has increased public acceptance of the 
technology over time, concerns about public reaction still 


App. 15 


—— 


existed when Geier’s 1987 Honda was manufactured. Fur- 
thermore, regardless of possible fluctuations in public accep- 
tance of airbags at that time, the concern about fostering the 
most effective passive restraint systems through experimen- 
tation remained. Therefore, “[b]jecause potential common law 
liability interferes with the regulatory methods chosen by the 
federal government to achieve the Safety Act’s stated goals,” 
Pokorny, 902 F.2d at 1123, Geier’s lawsuit claiming that the 
car she was driving was defectively designed because it 
lacked airbags is implicitly pre-empted.’ Accordingly, we 
affirm the grant of summary judgment to Honda. 


'? Contrary to Geier’s contention, our conclusion is not at odds 
with the position taken by the United States in prior Safety Act cases. The 
United States has previously contended that § 1392(d) “does not expressly 
or impliedly preempt design defect tort actions based on the claim that a 
vehicle was defective simply because it did not contain an airbag.” Brief of 
the United States as Amicus Curiae, on Petition for a Writ of Certiorari at 
7, Wood v. General Motors Corp., 494 U.S. 1065 (1990) (No. 89-46). But, 
the United States ultimately concluded that a no-airbag claim was pre- 
empted in Wood because the Department of Transportation specifically 
determined that “an all airbag rule would disserve the safety purposes of the 
Act” and that this policy “would be disrupted by tort liability, which 
therefore would be pre-empted.” /d. at 15 (emphasis in original). “If 
manufacturers are held liable for not installing airbags, . . . [a sizeable 
damage award against them] is likely to lead auto makers to install airbags 
in all cars. That outcome would obviously eliminate the diversity that the 
Secretary [of Transportation] found necessary to promote motor vehicle 
safety.” /d. at 13-14; see also Brief of the United States as Amicus Curiae, 
on Petition for a Writ of Certiorari at 28, Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 
U.S. 280 (1995) (No. 94-286).

MEMORANDUM 


Plaintiffs filed this action for negligence against 
Defendants for injuries arising out of an accident that 
occurred while Alexis Geier was driving a 1987 Honda 
Accord. Plaintiffs’ claim is based on the fact that the 1987 
Honda Accord was not equipt with an airbag. Defendants 
have filed a motion for summary judgment, arguing that such 
claims are pre-empted by the National Traffic and Motor 
Vehicle Safety Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1381 et seg. (now 49 U.S.C. 
§ 30101 et seg.) and the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety 
Standard 208, 49 C.F.R. §571.208. This motion is currently 
before the Court. 


Neither the issues raised by Plaintiffs nor the arguments 
presented by Defendants are novel. While these issues and 


App. 17 


arguments have caused a split among the many state courts 
and federal district courts that have looked at this question, 
the federal circuit courts have unanimously concluded that a 
cause of action for negligence based on the failure of a car 
manufacturer to install airbag during the 1980s is pre-empted 
by federal law. Harris v. Ford Motor Company, 110 F.3d 
1410, 1416 (9th Cir. 1997); Montag v. Honda Motor Co. Ltd., 
75 F.3d 1414, 1417 (10th Cir. 1996); Pokorney v. Ford Motor 
Co., 902 F.2d 1116, 1118 (3rd Cir. 1990); Taylor v. General 
Motors Corp., 875 F.2d 816, 828 (11th Cir. 1989); Wood v. 
General Motors Corp., 865 F.2d 395, 419 (ist Cir. 1988). 
Two other judges within this district have also found common 
law causes of action pre-empted by the national Traffic and 
Motor Vehicle Safety Act and the Federal Motor Vehicle 
Safety Standard 208. Wiley v. General Motors Corp., No. 96- 
1692, order granting summary judgment, (D.D.C. 1996); 
Hoftel v. General Motors Corp., 1988 WL 19615, *3 (D.D.C. 
1988). 


The Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, U.S. Const. 
art. VI, cl. 2, ensures that state law which conflicts with 
federal law is not given effect. The court should look to 
congressional intent when determining whether state law is 
pre-empted by federal law. Medtronic v. Lohr, 116 S. Ct. 
2240, 2250. The clearest expression of congressional intent is 
found in the language of the law itself as well as the 
“statutory framework” surrounding it. Jd. 


When examining the language of the National Traffic 
and Motor Vehicle Safety Act we see that § 1392(d) prohibits 
states from establishing “any safety standard” not identical to 
the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208 in effect at the 
time the vehicle is manufactured, which, in 1987, gave car 
manufacturers a choice as to whether to install airbags or not. 
Recovery on tort claims, such as that asserted by Plaintiffs, is 


App. 18 


equivalent to a safety standard promulgated by the state 
legislature or a state regulatory body. “State regulation can 
be as effectively exerted through an award of damages as 
through some form of preventive relief. The obligation to pay 
compensation can be, indeed is designed to be, a potent 
method of governing conduct and controlling policy.” 
Cipollone v. Liggett Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504, 521. Because 
the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208 demonstrates 
that “the Federal Government has weighed the competing 


interests relevant to the particular requirement in question, 


case or set of cases, and implemented that conclusion via a 
specific mandate on manufacturers or producers,” Harris, at 
1414 (quoting Medtronic v. Lohr, 116 S. Ct. 2240 at 2258), 
Plaintiffs’ claim seems to be pre-empted by § 1392(d). 
However, the court must also determine the import and effect 
of § 1397(k) of the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety 
Act which provides that “compliance with any Federal motor 
vehicle safety standard issued under this subchapter does not 
exempt any person from liability under common law.” At 
first, § 1397(k), the savings clause, and § 1392(d), the pre- 
emption clause, seem to be in direct conflict. However, 
reading these sections together in light of the Supreme 
Court’s pronouncements on the effect of common law 
regulation, it is clear that both sections can be given effect if 
the court finds that “compliance with Federal standards does 
not exempt anyone from any liability that the States have 
authority to impose.” Harris at 1415. The clearest example 
of this is common law liability connected with design defects. 
This persuasive reading of the language of the law 
demonstrates conclusively that Plaintiffs’ claim is pre-empted 
by federal law. 


The “statutory framework” as revealed in Congress’ 


App. 19 


entire regulatory scheme further supports the conclusion that 
Congress intended the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle 
Safety Act to preempt findings of common law negligence 
when manufacturers failed to install airbags in cars 
manufactured in 1987. Throughout the 1980s the Department 
of Transportation refused to require airbags based on a 
reasoned consideration of the long-term safety effects of such 
a mandate, hoping that even more effective and efficient 
occupant protection systems would be developed. 

For these reasons Defendants’ motion for summary 
judgment will be granted in an order accompanying this 
Memorandum.

William B. Bryant 
Senior United States District Judge

SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES 
October Term, 1998 


ALEXIS GEIER, et al., 
Petitioners, 


v. 


AMERICAN HONDA MOTOR CO., INC., et al., 


Respondents. 


On Petition for a Writ of Certiorari To The United States 
Court of Appeals For the District of Columbia Circuit 


RESPONDENTS’ BRIEF IN OPPOSITION 
TO PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI 


RESPONDENTS’ BRIEF IN OPPOSITION 


Joining five other circuit courts, the District of 
Columbia Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that 
petitioners’ no-airbag tort claim was impliedly preempted by 
federal law because such tort claims conflict with the method 
chosen by the federal government to achieve the goals of the 
National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966 (“the 


2 


Safety Act”). In particular, the Court of Appeals carefully 
reviewed the federal regulatory scheme, and recognized that 
common law no-airbag tort claims would frustrate the 
federal government’s policy of encouraging (1) public 
acceptance of airbags, and (2) “experimentation with better 
passive restraint systems.” App. 15. The Court of Appeals 
correctly concluded that a no-airbag claim is preempted 
because the Department of Transportation specifically 
determined that “an all airbag rule would disserve the safety 
purposes of the Act,” and that this policy “would be 
disrupted by tort liability.” App. 16. Moreover, the Court of 
Appeals correctly followed and applied controlling Supreme 
Court precedents governing federal preemption of state 
claims. Since this Court has repeatedly denied petitions for 
writs of certiorari on this precise issue, including as recently 
as last year, there is no reason for this Court to now exercise 
its discretionary powers in this case. See e.g. Irving v. Mazda 
Motor Corp., 136 F.3d 764 (11™ Cir. 1998), cert. denied, 119 
S. Ct. 544 (1998). Moreover, this case is not the right 
vehicle to resolve the FMVSS preemption issue inasmuch as 
the Court of Appeals never reached express preemption -- 

thus, a ruling in this Court could not resolve the entire 
preemption issue. Finally, changes in the law since the 
subject 1987 Honda Accord was manufactured require 
airbags in all new passenger cars beginning September 1, 
1997: therefore, this Court need not expend its judicial 
resources on this issue of diminishing importance.

vehicle accident that occurred on January 16, 1992, at 
approximately 10:30 p.m. in the 4900 block of MacArthur 
Boulevard, N.W. in Washington, D.C. Petitioner Alexis

On October 26, 1995, Honda moved for summary

Court of Appeals declined to decide the express preemption 
question “because we conclude that a verdict in [petitioners’] 
favor would stand as an obstacle to the federal government’s 
chosen method of achieving the Act’s Safety objectives, and 
consequently, the Act implicitly preempts [petitioners’] 
lawsuit.” App. 12. 


The Court of Appeals rejected petitioners’ claim that 
courts cannot reach implied preemption when there is an 
express preemption provision, relying on this Court's 
decision in Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 U.S. 280 
(1995). The Court of Appeals, after reviewing the regulatory 
history, concluded that “allowing design defect claims based 
on the absence of an airbag for the model-year car at issue 
would frustrate the Department [of Transportation’s] policy 
of encouraging both public acceptance of the airbag 
technology and experimentation with better passive restraint 
systems. Even if the Secretary’s gradual adoption of an 
airbag requirement has increased public acceptance of the 
technology over time, concerns about public reaction still 
existed when Geier’s 1987 Honda was manufactured.” App. 
15-16. Therefore, the Court held “because potential 
common law liability interferes with the regulatory methods 
chosen by the federal government to achieve the Safety Act’s 
stated goals,...Geier’s lawsuit claiming that the car she was

implicitly preempted.” App. 16. E 


B. The Safety Act and FMVSS 208 


4 In 1966, Congress determined that, given the 
centralized, mass production, high volume character of the 
motor vehicle manufacturing industry in the United States,” 
the country needed motor vehicle safety standards that were 
strong and adequately enforced” and "uniform 


manufacturing industry must fall squarely upon the Federal 
Government.” S. Rep. No. 1301, 89" Cong., 2d Sess. 4, 
reprinted in 1966 U.S. Code Cong. & Ad. News 2709, 2712. 


Accordingly, in 1966, Congress enacted the National 
Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1381 et 
seq. (“Safety Act”) (now 49 U.S.C. § 30101 et seq.). The 
Safety Act directs the Department of Transportation, through 
the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 
(“NHTSA”), to issue federal motor vehicle safety standards 
that are “practicable,” that “meet the need for motor vehicle 
safety,” and apply throughout the country. 15 U.S.C. § 
1392(a) (now 49 U.S.C. § 30111(a)). Federal motor vehicle 
safety standards must “protect against unreasonable risk of 
death or injury” in the event of an accident. 15 U.S.C. § 
1391(1) (now 49 U.S.C. § 30102(a)(8)). 


To ensure that the federal standards will not be 
undermined by application of a variety of state standards 


addressing the same features, Congress expressly preempted 
all non-identical state standards: 


6 
Supremacy of Federal standards... 


Whenever a Federal motor vehicle safety 
standard established under the subchapter is 
in effect, no State or political subdivision of 
a State shall have any authority either to 
establish, or to continue in effect, with 
respect to any motor vehicle or iteia of 
motor vehicle equipment, any safety 
standard applicable to the same aspect of 
performance of such vehicle or item of 
equipment which is not identical to the 
Federal standard... 


See 15 U.S.C. § 1392(d) (now 49 U.S.C. § 30103(b)). 
Explaining the need for this preemption, the House Report 
emphasized: 


[T]his preemption subsection is intended to 
result in uniformity of standards so that the 
public as well as industry will be guided by 
one set of criteria rather than a multiplicity 
of diverse standards. 


H.R. Rep. No. 1776, 89" Cong., 2d Sess., 17 (1966). The 
Senate Report stated that inconsistent standards are 
“preempted.” S. Rep. No. 1301, 89" Cong., 2d Sess., 12 
(1966). 


The Safety Act also contains a provision which 
makes clear that Congress did not intend to occupy the entire 
field of automotive safety (see 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k) 
{currently codified at 49 U.S.C. § 30103(e)]). As the Senate 
Report explained, this clause ensured that “compliance with 
such (federal) standards would thus not necessarily shield 
any person from product liability at common law.” S. Rep. 
No. 1301, 89 Cong., 2d Sess. 11, reprinted in 1966 U.S. 
Code Cong. & Ad. News (1966) (emphasis added). The 


7 


House Report also focused on compliance and defenses, not 
preemption [“compliance with safety standards is not to be a 
defense or otherwise to affect the rights of parties under 
common law particularly those relating to warranty, contract 
and tort liability”]. H.R. Rep. No. 1776, 89" Cong., 2d Sess. 
24 (1966). The role of § 1397(k) was not to negate 
preemption, but, as indicated in the Congressional debate, 
related to the evidentiary considerations of compliance with 
a safety standard. See 112 Cong. Rec. 21,490 (1966). 
Senator Cotton stated that “compliance with Federal 
standards may be offered in any proceeding for such 
relevance and weight as courts and juries may give it.” 112 
Cong. Rec. at 21,490 (1966). Senator Magnuson made the 
point that “[nJo court rules of evidence are intended to be 
altered by this provision.” 112 Cong. Rec. at 21,487 (1966).' 


In exercising the Secretary of Transportation’s 
authority under the Safety Act, the National Highway Traffic 
Safety Administration (“NHTSA”) has promulgated 
numerous standards on motor vehicle design and 
performance. FMVSS 208, the occupant restraint standard, 
addresses the “requirements for the protection of vehicle 
occupants in crashes.” 49 C.F.R. § 571. 208, $1. Its stated 
purpose te se the number of deaths of vehicle 
occupants, severity of injuries by specifying vehicle 
crashworthiness requirements in terms of forces and 
accelerations measured on anthropomorphic dummies in test 


: When Congress recodified the Safety Act in 1994, both

U.S.C. § 30103, entitled “Relationship to other laws.” Significantly, 
however, § 1392(d) was placed in 49 U.S.C. § 30103(b), labeled 
Preemption,” whereas § 1397(k) was placed in an entirely different 
subsection, 49 U.S.C. 30103(e), whose title (“Common law liability”) 
makes no reference to the Supremacy Clause or federal preemption. See 
Pub. L. 103-272, § 1(e), 108 Stat. 943. Since the petitioners and the 
Court of Appeals used the original statutory designations, we use them as 


well. 


crashes, and by specifying equipment requirements for active 
and passive restraint systems.” 49 C.F.R. § 571.208, $1.’ 


NHTSA first adopted FMVSS 208 in 1967, and 
required installation of manual lap belts in all new cars. 32 
Fed. Reg. 2415 (1967). The decision whether and when to 
require the installation of passive restraints, including 
automatic seat belts and airbags, has been the subject of 
extensive study, controversy, and modifications over the last 
three decades by NHTSA and Congress. See Motor Vehicle 
Mfrs. Ass’n. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 
(1983); State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Dole, 802 F.2d 
474 (D.C. Cir. 1986), cert. denied, 480 U.S. 951 (1987). 


In 1972, the Department of Transportation amended 
FMVSS 208 to require installation of passive restraints (air 
bags or automatic seat belts) for automobile manufactured 
after August 15, 1975. 37 Fed. Reg. 3911 (1972). For 
models built before that date, manufacturers could use 
manual lap and shoulder belts coupled with an ignition 
interlock. 


That standard had a short life. The public did not like 
ignition interlocks and made it known. Thereafter, in 1974, 
Congress abolished the “ignition interlock” standard. 
Congress also prohibited the Secretary of Transportation 
from issuing any standard requiring air bags or any other 
non-belt restraint system, among other things, unless the 
standard was submitted first to both houses of Congress and 
not disapproved by them. 15 U.S.C. § 1410(b), (c). 


Thereafter, every Secretary of the Department of 
Transportation rejected a mandatory air bag rule. In 1976, 


, “Passive” restraints are “devices that do not depend for their 
effectiveness upon any action taken by the occupant except that 
necessary to operate the vehicle.” Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State 
Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 34-35 (1983). 


9 

Secretary Coleman declined to issue a standard requiring air 
bags. He determined that air bags were very costly and 
might “cause or exacerbate injuries;” the public did not like 
or want them; they might precipitate “disastrous economic 
consequences for the whole nation;” and they provided no 
greater protection than seat belts when used. “The 
Secretary’s Decision Concerning Vehicle Occupant Crash 
Protection,” D.O.T. (Dec. 6, 1976), at 11-12, 32; 41 Fed. 
Reg. 24071 (June 14, 1976). 


In 1977, Secretary Adams also rejected an air 
only standard. Ho did issue a new FMVSS 208 requisite 
passive restraints, either air bags or automatic belts, to be 
rmsd som iles in 1981. He determined not to

1980s would have to be “completely redesigned” to 
accommodate them. 42 Fed. Reg. 34295 (July 5, 1977). 


In 1981, Secretary Lewis delayed Secretary Adams’ 
prospective passive restraint standard, and then rescinded it. 
46 Fed. Reg. 53419 (1981). The Secretary stated: 


The agency is also seriously concerned 
about the possibility that adverse public 
reaction to the cost and presence of 
automatic restraints could have a significant 
adverse effect on present and future 
acceptance of highway safety efforts. Id. 


In 1983, this Court vacated Secretary Lewis’ 
rescission decision, because the Secretary had not adequately 
set forth the reasons for it. This Court, therefore, remanded 
to the Secretary. See Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n. v. State 
Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983). 


Thereafter, Secretary Dole undertook “a thorough 
review” of all restraint systems, 49 Fed. Reg. 28962 (July 17, 


10 


1984), and reached a “final decision” respecting passive 
restraints. She determined to require a phase-in of them, but 
the phase-in was not to begin if states with two-thirds of the 
population enacted mandatory use laws (“MULS”) by 1989. 


The 1984 regulation provided a three-year lead time 
and phase-in to allow manufacturers an opportunity to 
provide more reliable automatic systems, and to permit 
consumers the opportunity to develop more information 
about the benefits of these systems. 49 Fed. Reg. at 29000. 
The phase-in schedule required a minimum of 10% of the 
1987 model year cars manufactured after September 1, 1986 
to use some type of automatic protection, but not necessarily 
airbags, 25% of the 1988 model year cars, 40% of the 1989 
model year cars, and 100% of cars from the 1990 model year 
and later. Id. at 28999. “By starting off with a relatively 
small percentage and building up to full compliance, the 
phase-in will provide the manufacturers with a better 
opportunity to manage unforeseen development and 
production problems and, as a result, also make it less likely 
that consumers will develop adverse impressions based upon 
earlier experience.” Id. at 29000. Secretary Dole explained 
that the phase-in was necessary because of “the need for the 
public to become accustomed to the technology and the need 
for protection, and [because] an across-the-board mandate 
too quickly could engender adverse public reaction.” Id. at 
28989. 


Secretary Dole found “a number of reasons” not to 
require air bags, id. at 29000, including: (1) “An air bag 
alone is less effective” than three point seat belts when used. 
Id. at 28986; (2) Air bags are costly, and are especially costly 
to replace. Id. at 29001; (3) Air bags may cause injuries, 
especially to children. Id. at 28992, 29001; (4) The public 
fears air bags and may not accept them; (5) Doubts about 
the efficacy of air bags (particularly in smaller cars). Id. at 
28974, 29001; and (6) “(By) restricting the manufacturers (to 


lal et i ie no- —w 


11 


air bags), the Department runs the risk of killing or seriously 
ing dev of more effective, efficient 


protection systems.” Id. at 29001 (emphasis added). 


To allay public concerns, Secretary Dole encouraged 
manufacturers to offer consumers a choice between 
automatic safety belts and airbags. The Secretary noted that 
“[iJt may be easier to overcome these [public] concerns if 
airbags are not the only way of complying with an automatic 
occupant protection requirement. Under the rule being 
issued, if people have concerns about airbags, they can 
purchase automobiles that use automatic belts.” 49 Fed. 
Reg. at 29001. 


Despite an attack on the Secretary’s rejection of a 
mandatory airbag standard, the 1984 standard was upheld as 
a careful balancing of policy interests. See State Farm Mut. 
Auto. Ins. Co. v. Dole, 802 F.2d 474 (D.C. Cir. 1986), cert. 
denied, 480 U.S. 951 (1987). The Court approved the 
Secretary of Transportation’s reliance on cost-benefit 
analysis and concerns about public acceptability (including 
fears about chemicals used to deploy airbags and the 
possibility of inadvertent deployment), reasoning that this 
analysis is “most appropriately entrusted to the expertise of 
an agency.” 802 F.2d at 488. 


In the years before the 1987 Honda Accord at issue 
was manufactured, NHTSA continued to refuse to mandate 
airbags. The agency denied a petition to reconsider the 1984 
regulation, stating “Standard No. 208 does not now require, 
nor has it ever required, manufacturers to install air bags in 
their cars...Instead...any restraint system that provides the 
specified performance may be used to comply with the 
standard” (52 Fed. Reg. 42440, 42445 [1987]). Another 
challenge to the rule was rejected the year after this vehicle 
was manufactured. The agency was held to have reasonably 


12 


considered long-term safety effects in its decision. See 
Public Citizen v. Steed, 851 F.2d 444 (D.C. Cir. 1988). 


In the 1987 model year, applicable here, Congress 
granted the manufacturer three options as to what restraints 
to install. In this vehicle, Honda chose the federally granted 
option of lap and shoulder belts with belt warnings. See 49 
C.F.R. 571.208, $4.1.2.3. (1987). 


On December 18, 1991, Congress enacted the 
Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991 
("ISTEA”). See Pub. L. No. 102-240. Congress directed 
NHTSA to amend FMVSS 208 to require, for the first time, 
airbags in 95% of 1997-model automobiles and 100% of 
1998-model automobiles. NHTSA’s final rule implementing 
this provision of ISTEA was promulgated in 1993. See 58 
Fed. Reg. 46551. Prior to this amendment, NHTSA 
informed Congress that “most courts that have considered 
the matter have ruled that [no air bag] claims are preempted 
by the...Safety Act and/or the safety standards issued by 
NHTSA.” — See letter to Congress from NHTSA 
Administrator Jerry Curry, dated November 7, 1991. 
Congress responded by specifying that: 


Nothing in this section or in the amendments 
made under this section to [FMVSS] 208 
shall be construed by any court as indicating 
an intention by Congress to effect, change or 
modify in any way the liability, if any, of a 
motor vehicle manufacturer under applicable 
law relative to vehicles with or without 
inflatable restraints. 


Pub. L. No. 102-240 § 2508(d).

continues. In 1997, NHTSA announced the need to

D. Due to the Change in Federal Law 
Mandating Airbags, the Issue of FMVSS 


Petitioners suggest that the FMVSS preemption issue 
is somehow increasing in importance. We strongly disagree. 
The ever-evolving nature of FMVSS 208, and the changes in 
the law as it relates to airbag technology, demonstrate that 
the claims presented by petitioners will surely fall by the 
wayside as vehicles manufactured without airbags cease to 
be driven. Petitioners greatly exaggerate the number of 
future no-airbag claims. Pet. At 11. All cars manufactured 
after September 1, 1997 are required to have airbags. App. 
3. In addition, numerous manufacturers before that time 
voluntarily equipped their cars with airbags. Consequently, 
the number of remaining no-airbag suits has steadily 
declined during the phase-in period and will continue to do 
so. 


In any event, this Court should not exercise its 
discretionary powers to render a decision based on a phase-in 
regulation that has since been replaced with a permanent rule 
mandating airbags in all vehicles. Where the statute or 
regulation upon which a controversy rests has been amended 
in a manner which prevents the problem from arising in the 


19 


future, certiorari should be denied. See Robert L. Stern, et 
al., Supreme Court Practice 172 (7" ed., 1993).°

Petitioners spend much of their Petition (Pet. 13-20) 
arguing that this Court’s decision in Cipollone v. Liggett 
Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504 (1992) radically changed federal 
preemption law and precludes resort to implied preemption 
analysis in the face of an express preemption clause. But 
this Court unanimously rejected this position as “without 
merit” in Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 U.S. 280, 287 
(1995); see also Medtronic, Inc. v. Lohr, 518 U.S. 470, 503 
(1996) [rejecting express preemption argument but stating 
that tort claim might “be under conflict 
preemption analysis”]. The Myrick court held that “the fact 
that an express definition of the preemptive reach of a statute 
‘implies’ - - i.e., supports a reasonable inference - - that 
Congress did not intend to preempt other matters does not 
mean that the express clause entirely forecloses any 
possibility of implied preemption.” The Myrick court noted 
(1) that in Cipollone, “we engaged in a conflict preemption 
analysis of the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising 
Act,” and (2) “our subsequent decisions have not read 
Cipollone to obviate the need for analysis of an individual 
statute’s preemptive effects. See, ¢.g., CSX Transportation, 
Inc. v. Easterwood, 507 U.S. 658 (1993).” Myrick, 514 U.S. 
at 288-89. Finally, the Myrick court actually applied the 
traditional implied preemption test - whether the lawsuit 
frustrates “the accomplishment and execution of the full 
purposes and objectives of Congress.” Id. Since there was 
no federal antilock braking standard, there were “no federal 
objectives or purposes” to undermine. Id. Simply put, in 


ae we 


ee ee er i ee re 


21 
1996, this Court considered implied preemption under the 
very same statute. The Court of Appeals could do no less. 


Petitioners’ contention is further undercut by this 
Court’s decision in Medtronic, Inc. v. Lohr, supra, where the 
defendant manufactured a pacemaker without any premarket 
review by the FDA, and needed to comply only with the 
FDA’s general rules regulating manufacturing processes and 
designs. A majority of this Court held that general FDA 
regulations applicable to all medical devices, as opposed to 
FDA regulations specific to a particular device, do not 
preempt common-law actions because there was no analysis 
by the federal government about the particular requirement 
in question. 518 U.S. at 501. However, a majority of this 
Court signaled that if there is a “substantive requirement for 
a specific device,” there is no need to reach the express 
preemption issue “if the claim would also be 
under conflict preemption analysis.” 518 U.S. at 503; see 
also 518 U.S. st 907 Gutlide Beuyer’s convuting opinion 
citing to “ordinary principles of ‘conflict’... preemption”). 


Nothing in the Cipollone opinion suggests that this 
Court overruled prior preemption decisions, or charted new 
ground. It is implausible that the Cipollone court intended to 
silently repudiate a long line of preemption decisions 
accepting implied preemption arguments regarding statutes 
with express preemption clauses. See e.g., Ingersoll-Rand 
Co. v. McClendon, 498 U.S. 133, 139 ( (1990); Jones v. Rath 
Packing Co., 430 U.S. 519, 540 (1977). Indeed, this Court, 
just six days before Cipollone, found implied preemption 
notwithstanding the existence of an express preemption 
clause. See Gade v. National Solid Wastes 
Ass'n, 505 U.S. 88, 104 (1992) (“the implications of the text 
of the statute evince a congressional intent to preempt non- 
er State regulations when a federal standard is in 
e .
