Subsequent decisions of this Court also demonstrate 
that there may be implied preemption in federal “oe ge 
express preemption clauses. See CSX_ Transp. _V. 
Easterwood, 507 U.S. 658 (1993); John Hancock Mut. Life 
Ins. Co. v. Harris Trust & Sav. Bank, 510 U.S. 86 (1993). 


In sum, the Court of Appeals properly determined 
that “the tension between §§ 1392(d) and 1397(k) prevents 
the identification of any ‘express definition’ of the reach of 
preemption in the Safety Act”; therefore “Cipollone does not 
bar this Court from considering Honda’s implied preemption 
argument.” App. 13. 


F. A Common Law Rule Requiring Airbags 
in 1987 Vehicles Would Destroy The 
Options and Flexibility at the Heart of 
FMVSS 208 


The Court of Appeals rightfully recognized that the 
effect of allowing petitioners’ no-airbag claim to proceed 
would “frustrate the Department’s policy of encouraging 
both public acceptance of the airbag technology and 
experimentation with better passive restraint systems”. App. 
15. The Court analyzed the regulatory history, and noted 
that “a performance standard making airbags one of several 
options car manufacturers could choose to comply with the 
passive restraint requirements of standard 208, rather than 
mandating specific use of one safety device, would advance 
public safety in two respects, by allowing consumers to 
adjust to the new technology and by permitting 
experimentation with designs for even safer systems. 49 
Fed. Reg. at 28,988, 28,997.” App. 15. 


The District of Columbia Circuit, of course, is 
uniquely experienced in the analysis of federal regulatory 
schemes both in general and in the particular context of 
FMVSS 208. See e.g. Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n. of the 


23 


United States, Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 
U.S. 29 (i983); State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Dole, 802 
F.2d 474 (D.C. Cir. 1986), cert, denied, 480 U.S. 951 (1987); 
Public Citizen v. Steed, 851 F.2d 444 (D.C. Cir. 1988) 


{opinion by then Circuit Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg]. 


Petitioners’ asserted common law standard takes 
away the federally mandated options and flexibility. See 
Pokorny v. Ford Motor Co., 902 F.2d 1116 (3 Cir. 1990). 
In Pokorny, the Third Circuit held that allowing plaintiff to 
assert a no-airbag claim “frustrates the goals of the federal 
regulatory framework and undermines the flexibility that 
Congress and the Department of Transportation intended to 
give to automobile manufacturers in this area.” The 
Eleventh Circuit in Taylor v. General Motors Corp., 875 
F.2d 816, 827 (11™ Cir. 1989) similarly noted that, if no- 
airbag claims are allowed, this would “remove the element 
of choice authorized in Safety Standard 208,” would “take 
away the flexibility provided by a federal regulation” and 
would thus “frustrate the regulatory scheme.” 


Moreover, the District of Columbia’s decision is in 
harmony with a number of this Court’s decisions on 
preemption. See, e.g., American Tel. and Tel. Co. v. Central 
Office Tel. Inc., 524 U.S. 214 (1998) [preempting state law 
claims that sought to bar activity authorized by federal 
statute]; Barnett Bank of Marion County v. Nelson, 517 U.S. 
25 (1996) [preempting state law that prohibited activity 
expressly permitted by federal statute]; CSX Transp. Inc. v. 
Easterwood, 507 U.S. 658 (1993) [holding common law 
standard based on train speed specifically permitted by an 
applicable federal standard was preempted]; Fidelity Fed. 
Sav. And Loan Ass’n v. de la Cuesta, 458 U.S. 141, 156 
(1982) [finding preemption of common law claim seeking to 
prohibit use of due-on-sale clause explicitly permitted by 
federal statute]; Chicago and N.W. Transp. Co. v. Kalo Brick 
& Tile Co., 450 U.S. 311, 325-26 (1981) [holding that a state 


24 


could not use “the threat of damages” to prevent the 
defendant from doing that which the federal agency 
specifically allowed under its duly-delegated authority]. 


G. Section 1397(k) of the Safety Act Does 
Not Preserve Preempted State Claims 


_ Petitioners argue that there can be no preemption of 
any common law claim because of § 1397(k), which 
petitioners mischaracterize as an “anti-preemption 
provision.” Pet. at 25. Im fact, § 1397(k): (1) never 
mentions the word “preemption,” (2) never addresses the 
preemption clause, and (3) is located several sections apart 
from the preemption clause. While respondents have no 
quarrel with the rule that words in a statute should be given 
their plain and ordinary meaning, petitioners’ discussion of 
an “anti-preemption provision” goes well beyond the actual 
words of the statute. 


Section 1397(k) provides: 


Compliance with any federal motor vehicle 
safety standard issued under this subchapter 
does not exempt any person from any 
liability under common law. 


Several factors indicate that § 1397(k) was not 
intended to be a provision that relates to the issue of 
preemption. The Court of Appeals cited Harris v. Ford 
Motor Co., 110 F.3d 1410, 1415 (9™ Cir. 1997) for the 
proposition that “the most reasonable and plausible reading 
of § 1397(k) ... is that compliance with federal standards 
does not exempt anyone from liability that the states have 
authority to impose.” § 1397(k) merely negates the 
availability of compliance with all government standards as 
an affirmative defense to common law actions. See Gracia 
v. Volvo Europa Truck, N.V., 112 F.3d 291, 298 (7® Cir. 
1997); see also Wood v. General Motors Corp., 865 F.2d 


25 


395, 417 (1* Cir. 1988) [compliance is not a complete 
defense “on the merits of a defective design claim”). 


The narrow language of § 1397(k) - “compliance 
with any federal motor vehicle safety standard” - is much 
narrower than the two exceptions incorporated into Section 
1392(d), which are true savings clauses. Each of these two 
savings clauses (for enforcement of identical state standards 
and for vehicles bought for the state’s own use) begin with 
the clear traditional savings language, “Nothing in this 
section shall be construed.” The two savings clauses in 
1392(d) state: 


Nothing in this section shall be construed as 
preventing any State from enforcing any 
safety standard which is identical to a 
Federal safety standard. Nothing in this 
section shall be construed to prevent the 
Federal Government or the government of 
any State or political subdivision thereof 
from establishing a safety requirement 
applicable to motor vehicles or motor 
vehicle equipment procured for its own use 
of such requirement imposes a_ higher 
standard of performance than that required 
to comply with the otherwise applicable 
Federal standard (emphasis added). 


True savings clauses use broader language, not the 
narrow “compliance with” language of § 1397(k). See 
Wood v. General Motors Corp., supra. 865 F.2d at 401, n. 8, 
417-18." Moreover, as this Court has recognized, “the 


~ 


ani nek SUS USOT Mut. Life Ins. Co. v. Harris Trust &

states that the statute “shall not be construed to exempt or relieve any 
person from any law of any state which regulates insurance banking, or

structure of the statute at issue.” CSX Transp., Inc. v. 
Easterwood, 507 U.S. 658 (1993). Here, § 1397(k) appears a 
full five sections after 1392(d), evidence it was not intended 
to address preemption. § 1392(d) is entitled “Supremacy of 
Federal Standards.” §1397(k) makes no reference to the 
Supremacy Clause. This further reinforces the conclusion 
that 1397(k) was never intended to create a sweeping 
exception to Section 1392(d). 


Moreover, the legislative history demonstrates that 
the purpose of § 1397(k) was only to negate the evidentiary 
defense of compliance with federal standards [“compliance 
with federal standards may be offered in any proceeding for 
such relevance and weight as courts and juries may give it”] 
(112 Cong. Rec. at 21,490); [“This provision does not 
prevent any person from introducing in a lawsuit evidence of 
compliance or non-compliance with federal standards. No 
court rules of evidence are intended to be altered by this 
provision”] (112 Cong. Rec. at 21,487). Compliance as a 
defense on the merits, of course, is entirely different from 
preemption. See Wood v. General Motors Corp., supra, 865 
F.2d at 417. Moreover, the legislative history does not speak 
to conflict preemption, and does not “specifically address the 
status of conflicting design standards established through the 
mechanism of common law suits.” See Wood v. General 
Motors Corp., supra, 865 F.2d at 406. If anything, the

In sum, the Court of Appeals correctly determined

grant review. First, the federal courts of appeals and state 
courts of last resort are hopelessly in conflict over whether 
federal law preempts a claim that a car is defective because it 
lacks an airbag. Second, this conflict is partly attributable to 
this Court’s decision in Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 U.S. 
280 (1995), which created massive confusion over whether it is 
appropriate to consider implied conflict preemption where 
Congress’ plain language expressly preserves common law 
claims. Third, whether the Safety Act preempts common law 
claims is an important question of federal law warranting this 
Court’s review. 


In response, Honda argues that review should be denied 
because: (1) there is no serious conflict among the lower courts; 
(2) this Court has recently denied review in other Safety Act 
cases; (3) this case involves only the question of implied 
preemption; (4) the issue is not important because airbags are 
now required in all vehicles; and (5) the decision below is 
correct. None of these arguments withstands scrutiny. 


1. As explained in our petition at 7-13, there is in fact 
a deep split among the lower courts on the precise question 
presented in this case: whether a manufacturer may be sued for 
failing to install airbags in one of its vehicles. Honda attempts 
to minimize this conflict by arguing that only a “small number 
of state courts” have held that no-airbag claims are preempted 
by federal law. Opp. at 15-16. This is an understatement of the 
first order given that, in the last five years, five state courts of 
last resort have decided the question in a manner directly 
contrary to all five federal courts of appeals to consider the 
issue. Pet. at 7-9. 


Honda does not attempt to argue that these state court 
decisions are not truly in conflict with the federal rulings. 


Instead, it pretends that a state/federal split of this magnitude is 
insignificant given the unanimity of the federal courts of 
appeals. This, of course, is not the law. See Supreme Court 
Rule 10(a); Stern, Supreme Court Practice 7” Edition, § 4.9, at 
181 (1993). In fact, this Court has often granted review in 
preemption cases based on a conflict between federal courts of 
appeals and state courts of last resort. See, e.g., Cipollone v. 
Liggett Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504, 508-09 nn.2 & 3 (1992) 
(citing split between five federal courts of appeals and two 
highest state courts as basis for granting review of cigarette 
labeling preemption decision); Lewis v. Brunswick, 107 F.3d 
1494 (11th Cir. 1997), cert. granted, 118 S. Ct. 439 (1998) 
(granting review of boat safety preemption decision based on 
split between two federal courts of appeals and one highest state 
court). Thus, Honda’s argument that there is insufficient 
conflict below to warrant review here — where there is a much 
deeper split than gave rise to either Cipollone or Lewis — is 
simply unavailing.' 


Honda’s related argument that the conflict below does 
not warrant review because “[nJone of the[ | state courts have 
yet rendered a final decision that would properly invoke this 
Court’s jurisdiction under Jefferson v. City of Tarrant, 522 U.S. 
75 (1997)” (Opp. at 16) is equally meritless. Jefferson held that 
this Court lacks authority under 28 U.S.C. § 1257(a) to review 
a non-final, interlocutory decision rendered by a state court of 
last resort. See 522 U.S. at 81. Even if this doctrine would 


' Honda also attempts to portray the five state high-court decisions 
as insignificant, in part, by citing a string of lower court federal and state 
cases that have found preemption of no-airbag claims. But there are scores 
of lower federal and state court cases that reached the opposite conclusion, 
too. See generally Cellucci v. General Motors Corp, 706 A.2d 806, 812 n.4 
(Pa. 1998) (collecting cases); Cooper v. General Motors Corp., 702 So.2d 
428, 433-34 (Miss. 1997) (same). 


have prevented review of the five state high-court decisions 
finding no preemption, this Court clearly has jurisdiction under 
28 U.S.C. § 1254(1) to review the decision below rendered by 
a federal court of appeals. See generally Stern, Supreme Court 
Practice 7 Edition, § 2.2, at 40 (1993). Indeed, this Court has 
regularly reviewed decisions of federal courts of appeals in the 
court decisions required under Section 1257(a). E£.g., 
Medtronic, Inc. v. Lohr, 518 U.S. 470, 482-84 (1996) (medical 
device preemption case reviewed on defendant’s petition for 
certiorari prior to trial on remand). Thus, there is no question ~ 
that the Court possesses jurisdiction to review this case (and 
Honda does not contend otherwise). 


Honda’s finality argument also fails because, even if the 
State decisions were not final for purposes of this Court’s 
review at the time they were rendered, they are (and will 
remain) the law of the land in those jurisdictions absent an 
a liability patchwork among the state and federal courts but, in 
cases where a state court of last resort has disagreed with the

state or federal court. Compare, e.g., Wood v. General Motors 
Corp., 865 F.2d 395 (ist Cir. 1988), cert. denied, 494 U.S. 
1065 (1990) (holding implied preemption of no-airbag claims) 
with Tebbetts v. Ford Motor Co, 665 A.2d 345 (N.H. 1995), 
cert. denied, 516 U.S. 1072 (1996) (holding no express or 
implied preemption of same). This perverse result can only be 
remedied by review by this Court. 

2. Honda also makes much of the fact that this Court 
denied review in two recent cases involving preemption under 
the Safety Act. See Opp. at 16 (citing /rving v. Mazda Motor 
Corp., 136 F.3d 764 (11th Cir. 1998), cert. denied, 119 S. Ct. 


3 


544 (1998), and Gracia v. Volvo Europe Truck, N.V., 112 F.3d 
291, 297 (7th Cir. 1997), cert. denied, 118 S. Ct. 697 (1998)). 


First, Honda ignores that this Court did grant review in 
a recent Safety Act case — Freightliner Corp. v. Myrick, 514 
U.S. 280 (1995) — that, by all appearances, seemed to present 
exactly the same question as this case: whether the Safety Act 
preempts common law no-airbag claims. See Pet. at 11-17 & 
nn.7, 13. This Court ultimately decided the case on other 
grounds, leaving the preemption question for another day. 514 
U.S. at 287. Thus, as of 1995, this Court viewed the 
preemption question presented here as sufficiently important to 


warrant review. 


This Court’s denial of certiorari in two recent Safety 
Act cases does not signal a retreat from the decision to grant 
review in Myrick. First, Gracia was not even a no-airbag case; 
rather, it involved a defective windshield claim. See 112 F.3d 
at 293. Tellingly, the Seventh Circuit’s decision did not even 
mention (much less analyze or rely upon) any of the myriad 
federal or state decisions regarding airbag preemption. Equally 
important, Gracia is aberrational insofar as it holds that the 
Safety Act expressly preempts common law claims. See id. at 
298. (As explained in the petition at 9-10 & n.5, all but one of 
the federal courts of appeals to decide the question have 
concluded that no-airbag claims are impliedly — but not 
expressly — preempted by Standard 208.) Because Gracia was 
decided on express preemption grounds, the Seventh Circuit 
never addressed whether a court may properly consider implied 
conflict preemption in the face of a statute — like the Safety Act 
— that appears expressly to preserve common law claims. Yet 
that precise question is the core of the split between the federal 
and state courts in the airbag preemption cases. See Pet. at 10- 
11. Thus, Gracia did not even come close to presenting the 


4 


question presented here, rendering this Court’s denial of 
certiorari in that case wholly irrelevant. 


Irving was a similarly unsuitable vehicle for review. 
First, like Gracia, that case did not squarely present a claim that 
a vehicle was defective because it lacked an airbag; rather, the 
because the manufacturer failed adequately to warn of the risk 
of not using all components of the safety belt system. See 136 
F.3d at 767. Irving was also beset with procedural 
uregularities, including extensive uncertainty over whether 
certain claims had been preserved for review. See id. at 768-69. 
Thus, it is not surprising that this Court declined to select 
Gracia or Irving to resolve the question first presented — but 
ultimately left unanswered — by Myrick.’ 


Since Myrick, this Court has denied review in four other Safety 
Act cases — Tebbetts, 665 A.2d at 345; Montag v. Honda Motor Co., 75 F.3d 
1414 (10th Cir.), cert. denied, 519 U.S. 814 (1996); Zimmerman v. 
Volkswagen of America, Inc., 920 P.2d 67 (Idaho 1996), cert. denied, 520 
U.S. 1115 (1997); and Schlotz v. Hyundai Motor Co., 557 N.W.2d 613 
(Minn. Ct. App.), cert. denied, 522 U.S. 823 (1997). In Tebbetts, the 
respondent successfully opposed review on the ground that the New 
Hampshire Supreme Court's decision finding no preemption was the first 
ruling by a state court of last resort or a federal appeals court on the 
preemptive effect of the Safety Act since this Court clarified the limits on 
implied preemption in Cipollone and Freightliner — and that there was, 
therefore, no post-Cipollone conflict. Brief in Opposition at ii, Tebbetts, 
No. 95-709 (October Term, 1995). In Montag, the Tenth Circuit created 
such a conflict by finding preemption, but Ford successfully argued that 
review should be denied because the case was decided on alternative 
grounds and did not squarely present the preemption issue. Respondents’ 
Brief in Opposition at v, Montag (No. 95-1885). In Zimmerman and 
Schlotz, the auto manufacturers successfully opposed review on the ground 
that the cases involved lap belts rather than airbags and, in Sch/otz, that there 
was an independent and adequate state ground for the decision. 


‘Respondents’ Brief in Opposition at 10-14, Zimmerman (No. 96-904); 


Respondents’ Brief in Opposition at 1-2, Schlotz (No. 96-2032). Thus, none 
5 


3. Honda’s third argument is that review should be 
denied because “the entire preemption question is not before the 
Court.” Opp. at 17. In reality, as Honda knows, both express 
and implied preemption were squarely presented to ihe courts 
below. The district court held that petitioners’ claims were 
expressly preempted by the Safety Act. See App. 19-20. On 
appeal, petitioners argued that their claims were neither 
expressly nor impliedly preempted. The D.C. Circuit 
considered and addressed the express preemption question at 
some length, see id. at 8-12, acknowledging that the Safety 
Act’s “broadly worded savings clause . . . indicates that 
Congress did not wish to deprive plaintiffs of all their remedies 
at common law.” App. 11. Although the Cour. ultimately 
declined to resolve the express preemption question, id. at 12, 
ruling instead that petitioners’ claims are impliedly preempted 
by Standard 208, id. at 14-16, there is no question that both 
issues were presented below and preserved for review by this 
Court. 


Similarly, both express and implied preemption were 
encompassed within the petition and, therefore, properly 
presented to this Court. Supreme Court Rule 14.1(a) provides 
that “[o]nly the questions set out in the petition, or fairly 
included therein, will be considered by the Court.” The first 
question presented, by its terms, raises the entire issue of 
preemption; it does not separately mention, much less 
distinguish between, express and implied preemption. 
Moreover, the petition discusses both express and implied 
preemption at length — in reviewing the conflict among the 
lower courts, the confusion caused by Myrick, and the 


importance of the federal question presented. The petition even 
explains how the Safety Act’s plain language and legislative 


of these cases was a suitable vehicle for answering the question presented 
here: i.e., whether no-airbag claims are preempted by federal law. 


6 


history illustrate Congress’ intent expressly to preserve 
common law claims, thereby barring any resort to implied 
preemption analysis. See, e.g., Pet. at 23-24. Finally, the 
petition argues that, given the similarity between the Safety 
Act’s express preemption provisions and those of various other 
statutes, “[t]his case . . . presents the opportunity to resolve the 
broader question presented in all of these cases: whether a 
plainly worded savings clause appearing expressly to preserve 
common law claims may be disregarded to find preemption by 
virtue of a manufacturer’s compliance with minimum federal 
safety standards.” Jd. at 26. 


Well aware of these facts, Honda vigorously argues in 
its opposition that petitioners’ claims are both expressly and 
impliedly preempted. See Opp. at 24-28 (express), 19-24 
(implied). The entire question of preemption is, therefore, 
plainly before this Court. 


In fact, this case is particularly appropriate for review 
given that the D.C. Circuit’s refusal to decide the issue of 
express preemption is actually at the core of the conflict below. 
As explained in the petition at 10-11, the federal courts of 
appeals and five state courts of last resort fundamentally 
disagree on whether it is ever appropriate to reach the issue of 
implied conflict preemption in the face of statutory language 
appearing expressly to preserve common law claims. In the 
state courts’ view, a court is barred from even considering 
implied conflict preemption without first deciding whether the 
statutory language expressly preempts (or saves) common law 
claims. The federal courts, in contrast, reject this approach, 
holding that implied conflict preemption may exist even in the 
face of clear statutory language expressly preserving common 
law claims. Following this approach, the D.C. Circuit declined 
to resolve the issue of express preemption, finding implied 


At bottom, then, a central issue in this case is whether 
the lower court erred in refusing to decide the express conflict 
preemption issue. Honda’s attempt to twist this refusal into a 
reason to deny review is unavailing and should be rejected. 


4. Honda also argues that review should be denied 
because “[a]ll cars manufactured after September 1, 1997 are 
required to have airbags” (Opp. at 18) and thus the issue will 
eventually disappear. This argument is belied by Honda’s 
previous statements and is factually inaccurate. 


First, Honda’s claim of “diminishing importance” is 
flatly contrary to its amicus brief filed in support of the petition 
for certiorari in Ford Motor Company v. Tebbetts, No. 95-709 
(October Term, 1995). See Pet. at 21-22. In that brief, Honda 
and its fellow auto manufacturers asked this Court to review the 
New Hampshire Supreme Court’s decision on the ground that 
federal preemption of no-airbag claims “is an issue of 
exceptional importance affecting national automobile safety . 
... Id. The auto manufacturers added that there are “/iterally 
millions of automobiles on the road today that are not equipped 
with airbags,” and that “[l]itigation over the preemptive effects 
of [Standard] 208 has proceeded for a decade, with no end in 
sight. . .. Only this Court can put an end to this controversy.” 
Id. (emphases added). In light of these representations made 
only a few years ago in a case involving the identical question 
presented here, it is disingenuous at best for Honda to claim 
now that review is unwarranted and that “[p]etitioners greatly 
exaggerate the number of future no-airbag claims.” /d. at 18. 


Honda’s argument is also wrong on the facts. As Honda 
admits, federal law only required airbags as of September 1, 
1997. Cars, of course, often stay on the road for years and 
years. In fact, the automobile at issue in this case was 
manufactured over /2 years ago, yet petitioners are only now 


presenting their arguments to this Court. Thus, at a minimum, 
no-airbag claims will continue to be litigated for at least another 
decade — and probably much longer. Unless this Court 
intervenes, the chaos among the lower courts will continue and 
spread, with victims’ right to seek compensation depending 
solely on whether they happen to reside in a no-preemption 
jurisdiction. 


Finally, this case has ramifications far beyond the airbag 
context. ivot only is preemption an open question with respect 
to other types of cases arising under the Safety Act, e.g., 
Gracia, 112 F.3d 291 (windshields); Irving, 136 F.3d 764 
(manual lap belts), but the Safety Act’s express preemption 
provision and savings clause are strikingly similar to the 
language of many other statutes. See Pet. at 25. Thus, a 
decision in this case could affect preemption analysis in a broad 
range of cases far beyond the no-airbag context. Honda’s 
attempt to minimize the importance of this case is accordingly 
without merit.’ 


5. Honda’s last argument — that the lower court’s 
implied preemption decision is right — is not a reason for 
denying review. To the contrary, it starkly underscores the 
need for this Court to step in and resolve both the dispute and 
the massive conflict among the lower courts. Moreover, as 
explained above, five state courts of last resort have held that, 
in view of the Safety Act’s remarkably clear savings clause, it 


> Honda also argues that the decision below is “unsuitable for 
review” because petitioners’ car was manufactured during the phase-in 
period (1987-89) when manufacturers had to install passive protection 
systems in only a percentage of their new cars. Opp. at 19 2.6. This 
argument is meritless, since Standard 208’s options framework was in effect 
during the phase-in period and no court — including the court below — has 
ever held that the preemption analysis is any different with respect to cars 


is both unnecessary and improper to even reach the question of 
implied preemption in the context of no-airbag claims. If 
Honda is right, and these decisions fundamentally misconstrue 
this Court’s jurisprudence in Cipollone and Myrick, then surely 
the appropriate response is to grant review to resolve the 
conflict — not to sweep the split under the carpet. 


CONCLUSION 


The petition for writ of certiorari should be granted.

AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES 


American Honda hereby raises the following affirmative 
defense to plaintiffs’ Complaint. 


Defense No. 1 
(Failure to State a Claim) 


Plaintiffs Complaint fails to state a claim upon which 
relief can be granted. 


Defense No. 2 
(Abuse or Misuse of Product) 


All of the injuries and damages alleged by plaintiff were 
caused by abuse and/or misuse of the subject vehicle by 
plaintiff, plaintiff's decedent or third parties for whom 
American Honda is not and was not responsible. 


JA-69 


Defense No. 3 
(Contributory Negligence) 


All of the injuries and damages alleged by plaintiff were 
caused by the contributory negligence of plaintiff, plaintiff's 
decedent or third parties for whom American Honda is not and 
was not responsible. 


Defense No. 4 
(Intervening or Superseding Cause) 


All of the injuries and damages alleged by plaintiff were 
caused by the intervening or superseding acts and/or omissions 
of plaintiff, plaintiff's decedent and/or third parties for whom 
Amenican Honda is not and was not responsible. 


Defense No. 5 
(No Proximate Cause) 


There exists no proximate causation between American 
Honda's alleged acts and omissions and the alleged injuries and 
damages claimed by plaintiff, thereby barring any recovery 
against American Honda. 


Defense No. 6 
(Failure to Comply With Warranty) 


The plaintiff or other third parties failed to comply with 


the terms of applicable warranties thereby barring any recovery 
from American Honda for any purported breach of warranty. 


JA-70 


Defense No. 7 
Limitations) 


Plaintiff's claims are barred by the Statute of 
Limitati 


Defense No. 8 
(Alteration or Modification) 


All of the injuries or damages alleged by plaintiff were 
caused by the alteration or modification of the subject vehicle 
by plaintiff, plaintiff's decedent or third parties for whom 
American Honda is not and was not responsible. 


Defense No. 9 
(Assumption of the Risk) 


The injuries or damages alleged by plaintiff were caused 
in whole or in part by the decedent's assumption of the risk. 


Defense No. 10 
(Preemption) 
Plaintiffs’ claims are preempted by Federal law. 


Defense No. 11 
(Statutory Defenses) 


American Honda pleads all defenses available under the 
laws of the District of Columbia. 


WHEREFORE, American Honda hereby respectfully 
requests that the entire Complaint be dismissed with prejudice, 
that it be awarded its costs and attorneys’ fees, and such other 
and further relief as this Court deems just. 


JA-71

QUESTION PRESENTED 


Whether an automobile manufacturer’s compliance with 
a federal motor vehicle safety standard promulgated pursuant to 
the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, 15 
U.S.C. §§ 1381-1431 (the “Safety Act”), preempts state 
common law claims that an automobile was defectively 
designed because it lacked an airbag where (1) the Safety Act 
expressly provides that “[c]ompliance with any Federal motor 
vehicle safety standard . . . does not exempt any person from 
any liability under common law”; and (2) the federal safety 
aaahad was a performance standard that 
encouraged, but did not require, the installation of airbags in 
cars? .

OPINIONS BELOW 


The opinion of the court of appeals (Pet. App. 1-16) is 
reported at 166 F.3d 1236. The order of the district court 
granting defendants’ motion for summary judgment (Pet. App. 
17-21) is not reported. 


JURISDICTION 


The court of appeals entered judgment on February 5, 
1999. This Court granted the petition for a writ of certiorari 
on September 10, 1999. This Court has jurisdiction under 28 
U.S.C. § 1254. 


STATUTORY AND REGULATORY PROVISIONS 


This case involves the National Traffic and Motor 
Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1381-1431 (the 
“Safety Act”), and Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208, 
49 C.F.R. § 571.208 (“Standard 208”). Relevant portions of the 
Safety Act and Standard 208 are in an appendix to this brief.' 


STATEMENT OF THE CASE 


A. Introduction. Congress passed the Safety Act in 
1966 to reduce motor vehicle injuries and deaths. To achieve 
that goal, Congress authorized the federal government to issue 
minimum safety standards for motor vehicle performance. 15 
U.S.C. §§ 1391(2), 1392(a). At the same time, Congress made 
clear that “[c]ompliance with any Federal motor vehicle safety 
standard does not exempt any person from any liability under 
common law.” 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k). In keeping with this 
statutory directive, for 20 years after the Act’s passage, the 


' On July 5, 1994, Congress recodified the Safety Act “without 
substantive change.” Pub. L. No. 103-272, 108 Stat. 745, 941. The 
relevant recodified provisions are also set forth in the appendix. 


nation’s appellate courts unanimously agreed that common law 
claims are not preempted by the Safety Act or by federal motor 
vehicle safety standards.’ 


Against this backdrop, in 1984, the National Highway 
Traffic Safety Administration (“NHTSA”) amended the federal 
motor vehicle safety standard governing occupant restraint 
systems — Standard 208 — to include a performance requirement 
encouraging, but not requiring, the installation of airbags. 
Consistent with the Safety Act’s dictate, NHTSA never 
suggested that compliance with Standard 208 would preempt 
any common law claims involving airbags. To the contrary, the 
agency found that “the most effective system is an airbag plus 
a lap belt and shoulder harness” (49 Fed. Reg. 28962, 28986 
(1984)) and, in keeping with Congress’ express preservation of 
common law claims, specifically noted that “potential liability 
for any deficient systems” would help spur auto manufacturers 
to install the best system. Jd. at 29000. 


This lawsuit harmonizes well with Congress’ and 
NHTSA’s actions. Petitioners allege that Honda should have

and shoulder harness. The lower court nonetheless held that, 
even if this allegation is true and Honda would be held liable at 
common law, Honda is immune from suit solely because it 
complied with Standard 208. This ruling violates the plain 
terms of the Safety Act, misconstrues Standard 208, and 
improperly interferes with both the power of the states in our 
federal system and the power of Congress to establish the law. 


B. The Safety Act. Congress enacted the Safety Act 
in response to the deaths and injuries resulting from unsafe 
vehicles. See S. Rep. No. 89-1301, 89" Cong., 2d Sess., 1-2 
(1966), reprinted in 1966 U.S.C.C.A.N. 2709, 2709-10; H.R. 
Rep. No. 89-1776, 89" Cong., 2d Sess. 10-11 (1966). The 
Act’s sole stated purpose is “to reduce traffic accidents and 
deaths and injuries to persons resulting from traffic accidents.” 
15 U.S.C. § 1381. See also Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State 
Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 55 (1983) (“Congress intended safety to be 
the pre-eminent factor under the Act.”). 


To this end, Congress empowered the Department of 
Transportation to prescribe “motor vehicle safety standards” 
that “shall be practicable, meet the need for motor vehicle 
safety, and be stated in objective terms.” 15 U.S.C. § 1392(a). 
The Act further defines “safety standards” as “minimum 
standard[s] for motor vehicle performance or motor vehicle 
equipment performance. ...” 15 U.S.C. § 1391(2) (emphases 
added). In issuing these minimum performance standards, the 
agency is directed to consider “relevant available motor vehicle 
safety data,” whether the proposed standard “is reasonable, 
practicable and appropriate” for the particular type of motor 
vehicle, and the “extent to which such standards will contribute 


3 


to carrying out the purposes” of the Act. 15 U.S.C. § 
1392(f)(1), (3), (4). 


When it enacted the Safety Act, Congress was fully 
aware of the existence of state common law design defect 
lawsuits against manufacturers.’ For that reason, Congress 
explicitly addressed what it did and did not intend to preempt 
in two separate sections of the Safety Act: the preemption 
provision and the savings clause. The former does not mention 
common law claims. Rather, it states in pertinent part: 


Whenever a Federal motor vehicle safety 
standard established under this subchapter is in 
effect, no State or political subdivision of a 
State shall have any authority either to establish, 
or to continue in effect, with respect to any 
motor vehicle or item of motor vehicle 
equipment any safety standard applicable to the 
same aspect of performance of such vehicle or 
item of equipment which is not identical to the 
Federal standard. 


* See, e.g., Hearings on H.R. 13228 Before the House Committee 
on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, 89" Cong., 2d Sess. 1256-57 (1966) 
(“House Hearings”) (testimony of Representative Charles P. Farnsley 
regarding design defect litigation involving the General Motors Corvair); id. 
at 1315 (statement of Daniel P. Moynihan regarding Comstock v. General 
Motors Corp., 99 N.W. 2d 627 (Mich 1959)); id. at 1351 (statement of Mr. 
Maurice A. Gargell concerning Corvair design defect litigation); Hearings 
on S. 3005 Before the Senate Committee on Commerce, 89" Cong., 2d Sess. 
252 (1966) (testimony of Dr. Seymour Charles noting pendency of 100 
lawsuits challenging safety design of the Corvair). See also generally Kurt 
B. Chadwell, Automobile Passive Restraint Claims Post-Cipollone: An End 
to the Federal Preemption Defense, 46 Baylor L. Rev. 141, 178 n.223 
(1994). 


15 U.S.C. § 1392(d). 


The Safety Act’s savings clause, in contrast, expressly 
refers to common law. It provides that “Compliance with any 
Federal motor vehicle safety standard issued under this 
subchapter does not exempt any person from any liability under 
common law.” 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k). 


C. Standard 208. Standard 208 sets forth minimum 
performance requirements for the protection of vehicle 
occupants in crashes. See 49 C.F.R. § 571.208. The version of 
Standard 208 at issue here was promulgated in 1984, in 
response to this Court’s decision in Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n 
v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983). Under this rule, 
manufacturers were encouraged, but not required, to install 
airbags in their vehicles. (Current law, in contrast, requires 
airbags in all new vehicles. See 49 U.S.C. § 30127(b); 58 Fed. 
Reg. 46551 (1993)). Although this case involves the 1984 
amendments to Standard 208, a brief review of the Standard’s 
prior history is essential to understanding the purposes of the 
1984 rule. 


1. Regulatory History. As originally issued in 1967, 
Standard 208 simply required the installation of seatbelts in all 
automobiles. See State Farm, 463 U.S. at 34. However, “[i]t 
soon became apparent that the level of seatbelt use was too low 
to reduce traffic injuries to an acceptable level.” /d. NHTSA 
therefore began considering “passive restraint systems” that do 
not require any independent action by the vehicle’s occupant. 
Id. at 35. Two types of automatic protection emerged from the 
investigation: automatic seatbelts and airbags. /d. Ultimately, 
the agency’s investigation showed that these passive restraints 
were substantially safer than manual alternatives, potentially 
saving approximately 12,000 deaths and 100,000 serious 
injuries annually. /d. 


Based on these findings, in 1969, NHTSA proposed a 
rule that would have required the installation of passive 
restraints in automobiles. See id. After extensive rulemaking 
proceedings, during which the agency repeatedly amended the 
rule to require various sorts of passive restraints, see id. at 35- 
36, and the automobile industry waged “the regulatory 
equivalent of war against the airbag,” id. at 49-50, NHTSA 
suspended the passive restraint requirement in 1976. /d. at 36. 
Although Transportation Secretary William Coleman concluded 
that airbags were safe and effective, he decided not to mandate 
passive restraints because he expected that there would be 


“widespread public resistance to the new systems.” /d. at 37. 


Secretary Coleman’s successor, Brock Adams, reversed 
the decision and mandated the phasing in of passive restraints 
for mode! years 1982 to 1984. Jd. The two principal systems 
that would satisfy the standard were airbags and automatic seat 
belts; the choice of which system to install was left to the 
manufacturers. See id. Seven months before the first deadline, 
however, new Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis delayed 
and then rescinded that order “due to changed circumstances 
and, in particular, the difficulties of the automobile industry.” 
Id. at 38. Finding that most manufacturers would install 
detachable automatic seatbelts rather than the far-safer airbags, 
he ruled that the passive restraint requirement would defeat auto 
safety, because the automatic seatbelts would simply be 
detached. Jd. at 38-39. 


In 1983, this Court in State Farm held that the rescission 
of Standard 208 was arbitrary and capricious. /d. at 57. The 
Court was especially critical that, after deciding that detachable 
automatic seat belts would not work, NHTSA had not even 
considered requiring airbags as the only form of passive 
restraints. Jd. at 48. This was clearly arbitrary, in the Court’s 
view, because “the agency’s original proposed Standard 


6 


contemplated the installation of inflatable restraints [i.e. 
airbags] in all cars.” /d. at 46.‘ Since that time, the agency had 
reaffirmed “the life-saving potential of the airbag” as a highly 
effective form of passive restraint. Jd. at 47-48. “Given the 
effectiveness ascribed to airbags by the agency,” the Court 
wrote, “the mandate of the Act to achieve traffic safety would 
suggest that the logical response to the faults of detachable 
seatbelts would be to require the installation of airbags.” Jd. at 
48. Because “NHTSA’s . analysis of airbags was 
nonexistent,” id., the Court vacated the agency’s decision 
rescinding Standard 208 and remanded for further 
consideration. /d. at 57. 


2. The 1984 Rule. In the aftermath of State Farm, 
Secretary of Transportation Elizabeth Dole reinstated the 
passive restraint requirement, with a phase-in period beginning 
September 1, 1986, and full implementation required by 
September 1, 1989. 49 Fed. Reg. 28962 (1984).° Under the 
new rule, auto manufacturers could satisfy the passive restraint 
requirement “by using automatic detachable or nondetachable

requirement permitted compliance by means other than the airbag . . 
‘{tJhis rule was a de facto air bag mandate since no other technologies were 
available to comply with the standard.’” /d. at 46 n.11 (citation omitted). 


* Under the phase-in schedule, “a minimum of 10 percent of all 
cars manufactured after September |, 1986, must have automatic occupant 
crash protection. After September 1, 1987, the percentage is raised to 25 
percent; after September 1, 1988, it is raised to 40 percent; and after 
September 1, 1989, all new cars must have automatic occupant crash 
protection.” 49 Fed. Reg. 28999. The rule further provided that the 
requirement for passive restraints would be rescinded if, by the end of the 
phase-in period (April 1, 1989), mandatory seatbelt use laws (“MULs”) 
were passed by enough states to cover two-thirds of the U.S. population. /d. 
at 28963. This never occurred, and the MUL provision was ultimately 
deleted. See 58 Fed. Reg. 46563 (1993).

provide the necessary level of relief.” Jd. at 28996 (emphasis 
added). Thus, under this version of the rule (which applies to 
petitioners’ veb’ -le in this case), manufacturers were permitted, 
but not required, to use airbags in their vehicles.° 


Because this Court had found the prior Secretary’s 
decision arbitrary and capricious for failing to consider an 
“airbags only” requirement, Secretary Dole went to some length 
to explain why the agency was not requiring “airbags only” — 
instead of automatic seat belts and other types of passive 
restraints — in all cars. First, comparing the two, she said that 
“(although airbags may provide greater safety benefits, when 
used with belts, and potentially larger injury premium 
reductions than automatic belts, they are unlikely to be as cost 
effective.” Jd. at 29001. Second, Secretary Dole expressed 
concern that, due to public unfamiliarity with the technology, 
a government-mandated “airbags only” rule “could lead toa 
backlash affecting the acceptability of airbags.” /d. Third, 
Secretary Dole noted that several commenters “questioned the 
Department’s authority to issue an “airbags only” standard, 
claiming that it would be a ‘design’ standard.” Jd. She said 
that, “{e]ven if the Department could legally issue a 
performance standard that could only be met by an airbag under 
present technology,” doing so would create “a number of 
problems” and could “unnecessarily stifle innovation” in other 
types of passive systems, such as automatic belts and passive 


* The agency noted that airbag technology had already been 
employed by various auto makers at various times. See, e.g., 49 Fed. Reg. 
at 28965 (noting that, between “1973 and 1976, General Motors produced 
approximately 11,000 full-sized Chevrolets, Buicks, Oldsmobiles and 
Cadillacs equipped ‘vith airbags, . . . Ford installed airbags in 831 Mercurys,

22,000 airbag-equipped cars worldwide. /d. 


interiors. /d. For these and other reasons, the agency declined 
to mandate airbags in all vehicles. See id. 


The agency made clear, however, that systems that 
included airbags were the preferred option. Secretary Dole 
repeatedly emphasized that the safest system was precisely the 
one that the petitioners seek to prove was an available, safer 
design in this case: “the most effective system is an airbag plus 
a [manual] lap and shoulder belt.” Id. at 28986 (emphasis 
added). See also id. at 28984. The Secretary also emphasized 
that this was not merely the agency’s opinion; to the contrary, 
the auto manufacturers themselves acknowledged that “the 
combination of an airbag and manual lap and shoulder belts . . 
. [is] the most effective system of all.” Jd. at 28966. 


In keeping with these observations, the new rule was 
designed to encourage the development and availability of 
airbags. As NHTSA explained, “{ajutomatic occupant 
protection systems that do not totally rely on belts, such as 
airbags or passive interiors, offer significant additional 
potential for preventing fatalities and injuries, at least in part 
because the American public is likely to find them less 
intrusive; their development should be encouraged through 
appropriate incentives.” 49 Fed. Reg. at 28963 (emphasis 
added). 


The first such incentive was the use of a phase-in 
requirement that permitted manufacturers gradually to install 
passive restraints over a three-year period. Secretary Dole 
explained, id. at 29000 (emphasis added): 


If the Department had required full compliance 
by September 1, 1987, it is very likely all of the 
manufacturers would have had to comply 
though the use of automatic belts. Thus, by 


9 


phasing-in the requirement, the Department 
makes it easier for manufacturers to use other, 
perhaps better, systems such as airbags and 
passive interiors. 


The second incentive to “encourage the use of non-belt 
technologies during the phase-in period” (id. at 28997) was to 
give manufacturers “extra credit” toward their percentage 
requirement if they used “something other than an automatic 
belt to provide the automatic protection to the driver.” /d. at 
29001. Under the rule, “[ flor each car in which they do so [i.e., 
install a non-belt passive restraint, such as an airbag], they will 
receive credits for an extra one-half automobile toward their 
percentage requirement.” Jd. at 29000. Although the credit 
could be earned by non-belt passive restraints other than airbags 
(such as “passive interiors,” see id. at 28965), NHTSA 
“believe[d] that the primary system that would be used under 
this ‘extra credit’ alternative would be the airbag.” /d. at 
29000. This was desirable because “airbags should provide 
very significant safety benefits.” /d. The agency added that, 
“{e]ven though fewer cars would be equipped with automatic 
protection if extra credit is given for airbag automobiles,” the 
tradeoff was worth it because “airbags — when used with belts 
~ are very effective.” Jd. 


The final incentive identified by the agency to 
encourage the use of non-belt alternatives — such as airbags — 
was the threat of future liability imposed through the tort 
system. According to Secretary Dole, “[s]}ome commentators 
on the rule suggested that [auto] manufacturers would use the 
cheapest system [automatic seatbelts] to comply with the 
automatic restraint requirement . . ..” Jd. at 29000. In response, 
she stated that “the Department does not agree with this 
contention. It believes that competition, potential liability for 
any deficient systems, and pride in one’s product would prevent 


10 


this.” Jd. (emphasis added). Thus, the agency believed that 
“potential liability” could create an incentive for manufacturers 
to avoid the cheapest passive restraint systems in favor of safer 
alternatives — such as the one the agency identified as the safest 
alternative of all: “an airbag plus a lap and shoulder belt.” 49 
Fed. Reg. at 28986. 


In keeping with this third incentive, the preamble to the 
1984 rule contains no indication that the agency sought to 
preempt any common law tort claims involving airbags or any 
other type of occupant restraint. To the contrary, in addition to 
the remark noted above, Secretary Dole explicitly noted 
comments that the auto manufacturers could be sued by crash 
victims who were injured because their cars lacked airbags: 


Another potential source of manufacturer 
liability was raised by Stephen Teret, 
representing the National Association for Public 
Health Policy: 


“If a reasonable means of protection is being 
denied to the motoring public, the denial should 
lead to liability, even if the liability can be 
imposed on each and every car manufacturer. 
People whose crash injury would have been 
averted had the car been equipped with an air 
bag can sue the car manufacturer to recover the 
dollar value of the injury.” 


Id. at 28972. See also id. at 28971 (discussing various 
comments relating to potential product liability claims 
involving airbags under the 1984 rule). Thus, the agency was 
aware of the possibility of future damage actions involving 
airbags, yet it never suggested that such claims would conflict 


ll 


with the 1984 version of Standard 208 — or that such claims 
would be preempted. 


D. This Litigation. In 1992, Alexis Geier was driving 
a 1987 Honda Accord in the District of Columbia. J.A. 2. At 
the time the vehicle was manufactured, Standard 208 required 
Honda to install some form.of passive restraint in at least 10 
percent of its cars (see n.5, supra), and permitted Honda to 
install passive restraints (including airbags) in all of its cars. 
Honda elected not to install any passive restraint in the vehicle 
driven by Ms. Geier; rather, her car contained the type of 
system — a manual three-point lap belt and shoulder harness — 
that was still permitted by Standard 208 during the phase-in 
period, but would be legally barred thereafter. 


At the time of the accident, Ms. Geier was wearing the 
lap belt and shoulder harness provided for the driver in the 
design of the car. Rounding a curve, the vehicle spun out of 
control and collided with a tree. The lap belt and shoulder 
harness did not adequately protect Ms. Geier, and she sustained 
multiple serious injuries. J.A. 2-5. 


On January 12, 1995, Ms. Geier and her parents filed 
this lawsuit seeking damages against Honda under the common 
law of the District of Columbia on theories of negligence, 
breach of warranty, and strict product liability. J.A. 5-42. 
Petitioners allege that the 1987 Honda Accord was negligently 
and defectively designed because it lacked “an effective and 
safe passive restraint system, including, but not limited to 
airbags ...” (J.A. 3-4), and that, if the car had contained a 
driver’s-side airbag in addition to the manual lap belt and 
shoulder harness, Ms. Geier would not have been seriously 
injured in the crash. 


12 


Even though the design advocated by petitioners was 
fully consistent with Standard 208 (and was the safest option 
identified by NTHSA in the preamble to the rule), Honda 
moved for summary judgment on the ground that the Geiers’ 
claims are preempted by the Safety Act and Standard 208. Pet. 
App. 17. The district court granted the motion and the court of 
appeals affirmed, holding that petitioners’ claims were 
impliedly preempted because they conflict with the goals of 
Standard 208. Pet. App. 17-20. 


The appeals court first acknowledged it would be 
“problematic” to find petitioners’ claims expressly preempted 
in light of both the Act’s “broadly worded savings clause” and 
the strong presumption against finding express preemption of 
common law claims when Congress’ intent to preempt “is not 
clear from the statute’s language.” Pet. App. 10-11. Given the 
broad wording of the savings clause, the court reasoned, “‘it 
would be difficult to discern a ‘clear and manifest purpose of 
Congress’ to preempt a design defect claim based on the 
absence of an airbag.” Pet. App. 11 (citations omitted). 


The lower court ultimately decided that it need not 
resolve the express preemption question, however, since it 
instead found implied preemption of petitioners’ claims. Pet. 
App. 12. The court first rejected petitioners’ assertion that, 
under Cipollone v. Liggett Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504 (1992), 
the Safety Act’s clear express preemption provisions preclude 
any inquiry into implied preemption. App. 14. The court went 
on to hold that petitioners’ claims are “implicitly preempted” on 
the ground that they conflict with the regulatory framework 
established by Standard 208. App. 16. While conceding that 
the 1984 rule “does not mandate or forbid the use of airbags” 
(Pet. App. 14), the court held that imposition of common law 
liability for failure to instali an airbag would frustrate the 
federal government’s goals of “encouraging both public 


13 


acceptance of the airbag technology and experimentation with 
better passive restraint systems.” Pet. App. 15. Thus, the court 
concluded, Ms. Geier had no right to seek compensation for her 
injuries at common law. : 


SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT 


In determining whether a state cause of action is 
preempted by federal law, the Court’s sole task is to ascertain 
the intent of Congress. This determination of Congressional 
intent is not made in a vacuum; rather, it is informed by a strong 
presumption against preemption that can be overcome only by 
a clear manifestation of congressional intent to the contrary. 


Measured in this light, it is clear that Congress did not 
intend to preempt common law tort claims under the Safety 
Act. Indeed, the two provisions of the Safety Act that set forth 
Congress’s intent with respect to preemption — the preemption 
provision (15 U.S.C. § 1392(d)) and the savings clause (15 
U.S.C. § 1397(k)) — reveal that common law claims are 
expressly preserved, not preempted. 


The language of the preemption provision shows that 
Congress only intended to preempt state Jegislative or 
administrative safety standards that are not identical to federal 
safety standards governing the same aspect of motor vehicle 
performance, and not to preempt common law tort actions. 
Thus, the Safety Act’s express preemption provision does not 
even encompass common law tort claims. 


Any doubt on this point would be dispelled by the 
savings clause, which states in sweeping and unambiguous 
terms that “compliance with any . . . safety standard . . . does 
not exempt any person from any liability under common law.” 
Both the plain language of this “anti-preemption” provision and 


14 


its legislative history leave no room for a conclusion that 
petitioners’ claims are expressly preempted by the Safety Act. 


Nor are petitioners’ claims impliedly preempted by the 
Safety Act. This Court has made clear that, where Congress has 
spoken directly and clearly on the issue of preemption — as it 
did in the Safety Act — there can be no finding of implied 
preemption. Because the Safety Act contains both an express 
preemption provision and an express anti-preemption provision 
manifesting a congressional intent not to preempt, any inquiry 
into implied conflict preemption is precluded. Thus, all of 
Honda’s arguments about the alleged conflict between 
petitioners’ claims and Standard 208 are irrelevant. 


Even assuming, however, that this Court could reach the 
issue of implied conflict preemption in this case, there is no 
preemption here since petitioners’ claims do not conflict with 
the Safety Act or Standard 208. Implied conflict preemption 
applies only where it is impossible for a private party to comply 
with both state and federal requirements or where state law 
would frustrate the full purposes and objectives of Congress. 
Impossibility is not an issue in this case, since Standard 208 
undisputably would have permitted installation of an airbag in 
Ms. Geier’s 1987 Honda and, in any event, would allow Honda 
to pay damages to the Geiers. 


Similarly, petitioners’ claims do not frustrate any federal 
purpose. First, this lawsuit does not frustrate any Congressional 
purpose, since Congress made clear (in the Act’s savings 
clause) that the preservation of common law claims would aid 
the accomplishment and execution of its full purposes. 
Congress recognized that federal regulations and common law 
liability can and should work together to create safer vehicles. 
Given Congress’ expressed desire to preserve all common law 
claims, petitioners’ claims would not frustrate the purpose of 


15 


the Safety Act. But a finding of implied preemption here 
would. 


Petitioners’ claims are also consistent with the goals 
underlying Standard 208. As Congress intended, NHTSA 
promulgated Standard 208 as a minimum performance standard 
and left the common law undisturbed. NHTSA noted, however, 
that the “most effective” system was “an airbag plus a lap belt 
and shoulder harness,” 49 Fed. Reg. at 28986, and explicitly 
relied on several incentives to encourage the use of airbags — 
including the threat of “potential liability for any deficient 
system.” Jd. at 29000. Petitioners’ attempt to hold Honda 
liable for failing to install an airbag (in addition to a manual lap 
belt and shoulder harness) in the 1987 Honda Accord is in 
perfect harmony with this approach. 


Finally, contrary to the lower court’s ruling, petitioners’ 
claims do not frustrate the goals identified by NHTSA in its 
1984 rule of “allowing consumers to adjust to the new [airbag] 
technology” and “permitting experimentation with designs for 
even safer systems.” Pet. App. 15. Regarding the former, the 
agency declined to require airbags in all cars by administrative 
fiat partly because it feared a public backlash. No such 
backlash would result from common law liability in a no-airbag 
suit, however, both because a manufacturer would not likely 
change its conduct in response to a jury verdict and because, 
even if the manufacturer did, it would make every effort to 
promote public acceptability of airbags. This lawsuit is also in 
line with NHTSA’s goal of promoting technological 
experimentation, since (as Secretary Dole recognized) the 
common law tort system actually encourages manufacturers to 
experiment with safer product designs. Because petitioners’ 
claims are entirely consistent with — and actually advance — the 
goals underlying Standard 208, the lower court’s finding of 
implied conflict preemption is in error. 


16 


ARGUMENT 


This case is about federalism and the separation of 
powers. For decades, this Court has emphasized that federal 
preemption analysis is governed by two bedrock legal 
principles based on these Constitutional concerns. 


First, as the Court recently reaffirmed in Medtronic v. 
Lohr, 518 U.S. 470, 485 (1996), a party seeking preemption of 
state law bears a heavy burden of overcoming the long-standing 
“presum[ption] that Congress does not cavalierly pre-empt 
state-law causes of action.” In all preemption cases, a court 
must start with an assumption “that the States’ historic police 
powers cannot be superseded by a Federal Act unless that is 
Congress’ clear and manifest purpose.” /d. (citation omitted). 
These are not empty platitudes; they stem from and protect our 
Constitutional system of federalism. See, e.g., Jones v. Rath 
Packing, 430 U.S. 519, 525 (1977) (the presumption against 
preemption “provides assurance that ‘the federal-state balance’ 
. will not be disturbed unintentionally by Congress or 
unnecessarily by the courts.”’) (citation omitted). 


This presumption is especially strong where, as in this 
case, preemption would displace the historic power of the states 
to protect the health and safety of their citizens. See Medtronic, 
518 U.S. at 485. Moreover, where preemption of common law 
claims would leave injured individuals without any state or 
federal remedy, which is the result sought by Honda here, a 
court may find preemption only in the most compelling 
circumstances. See English v. General Electric Corp.,496 U.S. 
72, 87-90 (1990); Silkwood v. Kerr-McGee Corp., 464 U.S. 
238, 251 (1984). 


Second, in determining whether a state cause of action 
is preempted by federal law, the Court’s “sole task is to 


17 


ascertain the intent of Congress.” California Fed. Sav. & Loan 
Ass'n vy. Guerra, 479 U.S. 272, 280 (1987) (plurality). This 
principle, too, is Constitutionally-based; it derives from and 
preserves the separation of powers, limiting the courts to their 
Constitutionally-assigned role. As long as Congress acts within 
the scope of its powers, the courts must stay true to Congress’ 
intent. They are not free to use the doctrine of implied 
preemption (or anything else) to substitute their judgment for 
that of Congress. 


I, Petitioners’ Claims Are Not Expressly Preempted 
And, In Fact, Are Expressly Preserved. 


The provisions of the Safety Act that set forth Congress’ 
intent regarding preemption — the preemption provision (15 
U.S.C. § 1392(d)) and the savings clause (15 U.S.C. § 1397(k)) 
— reveal that common law claims are expressly preserved, not 
preempted. 


A. The Preemption Provision Does Not 
Encompass Common Law Claims. 


The Safety Act’s preemption provision states in 
pertinent part: 


Whenever a Federal motor vehicle safety 
standard established under this subchapter is in 
effect, no State or political subdivision of a 
State shall have any authority either to establish, 
or to continue in effect, with respect to any 
motor vehicle or item of motor vehicle 
equipment any safety standard applicable to the 
same aspect of performance of such vehicle or 
item of equipment which is not identical to the 
Federal standard. 


18 


15 U.S.C. § 1392(d). 


The most notable feature of this language is the absence 
of any reference at all to common law claims. Although the 
absence of an explicit reference to common law does not 
automatically preclude a finding of preemption, see Cipollone, 
505 U.S. at 520-22, the absence of such a reference in Section 
1392(d) combined with the express reference to “common law” 
in the Act’s savings clause, 15 U.S.C. § 1397(k) (discussed in 
more detail below), defeats any notion that Congress intended 
the Safety Act’s preemption provision to encompass common 
law claims. E.g., Chicago v. Environmental Defense Fund, 511 
U.S. 328, 337 (1994) (“It is generally presumed that Congress 
acts intentionally and purposely when it includes particular 
language in one section of a statute but omits it in another.”) 
(internal quotation marks omitted). Accord Keene Corp. v. 
United States, 508 U.S. 200, 208 (1993).’ 


Even putting aside the absence of any reference to 
“common law” in the preemption provision, however, many 
other aspects of Section 1392(d) and the Safety Act demonstrate 
that Congress never intended to preempt tort suits against auto 
manufacturers. 


First, the preemption provision only prohibits a State 
from establishing or continuing in effect a “safety standard” that 


” The absence of any reference to common law claims in the Act’s 
preemption provision would be telling even if the savings clause did not 
exist. Congress has repeatedly shown its ability to refer to “common law” 
when it intends to include it within the scope of a preemption clause. 
Compare, e.g., Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U.S.C. § 301(a) (1977) 
(preempting rights “under the common law, rule, or public policy”); 
Domestic Housing and Internationa! Recovery and Financial Stability Act, 
12 U.S.C. § 1715z-12, -18(e) (1989) (preempting any “State constitution, 
statute, court decree, common law, rule or public policy”).

conflicts with a “Federal motor vehicle safety standard” 
established under the Act. Although the term “safety standard,” 
standing alone, may not be wholly self-defining, it does not 
stand alone in Section 1392(d): rather, Congress used the same 
term in the same provision fwice to refer, in the first instance, 
to the type of federal law that is to be accorded preemptive 
effect — a “Federal motor vehicle safety standard” — and, in the 
other, to the type of state law that is subject to preemption — 
again, a “safety standard.” “Safety standard,” moreover, is the 
term used throughout the Act to refer to the administrative 
standards that the Secretary is authorized to adopt pursuant to 
the Act.* The use of the same term to refer to the state norms 
that may be displaced by a Federal “safety standard” is, under 
normal rules of statutory construction, indicative that the term 
is meant to have the same meaning. See Estate of Cowart v. 
Nicklos Drilling Co., 505 U.S. 469, 479 (1992) (It is a “basic 
canon of statutory construction that identical terms within an 
Act bear the same meaning.”) (citing cases); Morrison-Knudsen 
Const. v. Director, Office of Workers Comp. Programs, 461 
U.S. 624, 633 (1983) (“[A] word is presumed to have the same 
meaning in all subsections of the same statute.”). See also 
Medtronic, 518 U.S. at 489 (plurality opinion) (citing other uses 
of the term “requirements” thrc ughout statute to demonstrate 
that Congress’ focus is “enactments of positive law by 
legislative or administrative bodies, not the application of 
general rules of common law by judges and juries”). Thus, the 
only sensible reading of the Safety Act’s preemption provision

is that a “safety standard” promulgated under the Act will only 
preempt a state legislative or administrative “safety standard” 
that is not identical to the federal standard.’ 


Second, the fact that Section 1392(d) limits the 
preempted field to state and local safety standards “with respect 
to” motor vehicles further demonstrates that preemption under 
the Safety Act is limited to state positive law. The tort duties 
respect to” motor vehicles, but rather are general state-law 
responsibilities concerning the conduct of persons who 
manufacture and sell all kinds of products. On the other hand, 
state positive-law requirements to which the preemption 
provision is directed are, in fact, standards “with respect to” 
motor vehicles. See Medtronic, 518 U.S. at 501-02 (rejecting 
preemption of common law claims on ground that “the general 
state common-law requirements in this suit were not 
specifically developed ‘with respect to’ medical devices. 
Accordingly, they are not the kinds of requirements that 
Congress and the [agency] feared would impede the ability of 
federal regulators to implement and enforce specific federal 
requirements.”’). 


Third, the “safety standards” referred to in the Safety 
Act’s preemption provision are “minimum standards” that 
concern an “aspect of performance.” This was not an idle 


* In this respect, the Safety Act is markedly different from the

choice of words by Congress. As the Senate Report

Unlike the General Services Administration’s 
procurement standards, which are primarily

to be performance standards, specifying the 
required minimum safest performance of
